create-a-world.title: Create a world
create-a-world.description: A world is the place where your 3D scene lives. One call creates it, and it draws into a canvas on your page.
steps: Get the engine. It is not on npm yet: clone the repository, run pnpm install and pnpm run build in it, then add it to your project from that folder.
Put a <canvas> in your page. A canvas is a rectangle of the page that a program can draw into. Give it a width and a height.
Call createWorld with the canvas id. You get a world: a scene (the list of things to draw), a camera (the eye that looks at them) and everything that draws the picture.
Add one cube and one light, so there is something to see. The next chapters explain these lines one by one.
When your page closes, call world.dispose() to give the memory back.
create-a-world.tryIt: Drag the picture to turn around the cube. Pick another colour in the panel.

add-a-shape.title: Add a shape
add-a-shape.description: Everything you see is a mesh: a shape with a material on it. Make the shape with `geometry`, wrap it in a mesh with `object.mesh`, and add it to the scene.
steps: A shape, or geometry, is only the form: its corners and its faces. geometry.box(1, 1, 1) is a cube one metre wide, geometry.sphere(0.75) a ball. There are also cylinders, cones, rings, tori and more.
A mesh is a shape plus a material: object.mesh(shape, material). The material is the next chapter.
Place a mesh with position, turn it with rotation and size it with scale. Rotations are in radians: a full turn is Math.PI * 2.
object.group() holds several meshes, so they move together, like the plate of the turntable.
Nothing shows until you call world.scene.add(mesh).
add-a-shape.tryIt: Change the colour of the shapes, stop the spin, or turn it faster.

give-it-a-material.title: Give it a material
give-it-a-material.description: A material says what a surface is made of: its colour, whether it is metal, how rough it is. `material.meshStandard` covers almost everything.
steps: color is the paint, written like a web colour: '#e8a25a'.
metalness goes from 0 (plastic, clay, wood) to 1 (metal). A metal shows the colours of what it reflects.
roughness goes from 0 (smooth like a mirror, with small sharp highlights) to 1 (rough like chalk, with soft light everywhere).
Change a material whenever you like: chrome.roughness = 0.3. Every mesh that uses it changes at once.
Glass is material.meshPhysical with transmission: 1: light goes through it. ior, the index of refraction, says how much it bends light: 1.5 for window glass. See it in Glass on the table.
give-it-a-material.tryIt: Each column is more metal than the one before, and each row is rougher. Pick one colour for all of them, and make the lamps brighter.

light-it.title: Light it
light-it.description: Without a light, everything is black. Add lights with the `light` family, and let them cast shadows.
steps: light.directional is the sun: all its rays go the same way, and position says where it shines from.
light.point is a bulb: it shines all around and fades with distance. light.spot is a torch: a cone of light.
light.ambient is a soft light from everywhere. A little of it keeps the shadows from being pitch black.
Add castShadow: true and what the light hits throws a shadow.
intensity is how strong a light is, color its colour. Change them any time: sun.intensity = 1.
light-it.tryIt: Move the hour: the sun crosses the sky, turns red at dusk, and every shadow turns with it.

move-the-camera.title: Move the camera
move-the-camera.description: The camera is your eye in the world. Place it in code, then let the reader move it with `world.controls`.
steps: world.camera.position.set(x, y, z) puts the eye somewhere; world.camera.lookAt(x, y, z) turns it towards a point.
A controller turns the mouse, fingers and keyboard into camera moves. Choose it when you create the world: createWorld('view', { controls: 'orbit' }).
'orbit' circles a point: drag to turn, right-drag to slide, scroll to zoom. world.controls.target is the point it circles.

There are others: 'fly' (keys W A S D, see A fighter jet in the canyon), 'character' (run and jump, bumping into walls, see Temple parkour), 'firstPerson' (walk through everything), 'trackball', 'panZoom' for a flat map, and 'none' when your code moves the camera itself.
Switch at any time: world.controls.kind = 'fly'.
move-the-camera.tryIt: Drag to turn around the clock, scroll to look closely at the teeth of the gears.

animate.title: Animate
animate.description: To make things move, give the world a function to run before every picture, with `world.onFrame`.
steps: The world draws a new picture many times a second. Each picture is a frame. world.onFrame(fn) runs fn before each one.
fn receives delta: the seconds since the last frame. Multiply your speeds by it, and things move just as fast on a quick screen as on a slow one.
Call world.invalidate() to say “draw again”. When nothing asks for a new frame, the world rests: a scene that does not move costs nothing.

For a motion made of poses, like a walk, use the animation mixer. animation.clip lists the poses and when they happen; animation.createMixer(robot).play(clip) plays them and fills in the moments between. See Blending robot motions.
animate.tryIt: Change the height and the speed of the wave. Double-click the floor to drop a new stone.

load-a-compiled-model.title: Load a compiled model
load-a-compiled-model.description: A model made in a 3D program is compiled once, then one line adds it to your world. The engine then loads only the parts the camera needs.
steps: Most 3D programs export glTF files (.gltf or .glb), the common format for 3D models.

The compiler cuts the model into small pieces called clusters, patches of about a hundred triangles, and saves each one at several levels of detail. Run it once, in a terminal: the model, the output folder, full to keep the whole model, a triangle budget, and the web address the folder will be served from.
Put the output folder on your web server, at that address.
In the page, await world.scene.load(url) adds the model. It gives back the model, with its size in bounds, to frame the camera.
The model is never downloaded whole. The engine fetches the pieces the camera sees, finer as you come closer. This is called streaming.
load-a-compiled-model.tryIt: Turn the lamp around the head, raise it, change its colour.

stay-within-memory.title: Stay within memory
stay-within-memory.description: A big model does not have to fit in memory. You give the engine a fixed amount, and it keeps what the view needs most inside it.
steps: The GPU, the chip that draws the picture, has its own memory, and a web page cannot ask how much of it is free. So you choose the amount yourself.
world.budget.geometryPool is the memory for shapes; world.budget.texturePool is the memory for the images painted on surfaces, called textures. Both are counted in bytes.
When the view needs more than the budget, nothing breaks: far and small parts are drawn with fewer triangles until everything fits. The picture stays whole, only less detailed.
Read the value back to see what the engine really holds.
See the pieces with world.diagnostic.mode = 'clusters': each cluster gets its own colour.
stay-within-memory.tryIt: Slide the memory down: the pieces grow bigger, the building stays whole. Choose clusters in the stats panel's View menu, bottom left, to see them.

make-things-fall.title: Make things fall
make-things-fall.description: Turn the physics on and your shapes gain weight: they fall, bump and come to rest.
steps: Give the world physics: true. The simulation runs apart from the drawing, in a worker, so it never slows the picture down.
Mark the floor 'static': it holds the others and never moves. Mark a box 'dynamic': gravity pulls it.
The shape comes from the geometry, the weight from the material: physics: 'wood' is light, 'metal' is heavy, 'rubber' bounces.
Push a body with applyImpulse, or listen to its contact. Once every body sleeps, nothing is computed and nothing is drawn.
A model loaded with scene.load collides with its own triangles, cooked when it was compiled. await world.raycast(point, { exact: true }) finds the very triangle under the cursor.
make-things-fall.tryIt: Drop more boxes, switch the gravity to the Moon, and turn on slow motion.

touch-and-react.title: Touch and react
touch-and-react.description: Walk into your world: with the physics on, the character climbs, rides and pushes what it meets, and what it meets pushes back.
steps: Create the world with controls: 'character' and physics: true. The character is now a body of the physics, like the boxes.
Mark what never moves 'static': the floor, the stairs, the walls. The character climbs steps up to its knee and slopes up to 45°.
Mark a platform 'kinematic' and move it from your code each frame: whatever stands on it rides along.
Make boxes 'dynamic' and light: the character pushes them with pushStrength newtons, and they fall, tumble and push back.
touch-and-react.tryIt: Click the picture, walk with W A S D, jump with Space. Climb the stairs, ride the platform, push the stack of boxes.

connect-drive-and-break.title: Connect, drive and break
connect-drive-and-break.description: Joints hold two bodies together, or a body to the world: a door turns on its hinge, a drawer slides on its rail, a chain hangs by its links, and a bridge breaks when pulled too hard.
steps: Make a joint with joint.hinge(a, b, options) or its kin — fixed, point, slider, distance, cone — and give it to world.physics.add. Put null for b to hold a body to the world.
anchor is where the bodies connect and axis the way the pin or the rail points, both in the world, read when the joint is made.
limits stop the joint: radians for a hinge, metres for a slider. A spring makes the stop soft.
A motor drives a hinge or a slider to a speed or a position. Change joint.motor at any time.
breakForce is the pull, in newtons, past which the joint snaps: joint.broken turns true and joint.on('break', …) is called.

Advanced joints tie motions together: joint.gear(a, b, { ratio }) turns two hinged wheels as one train, joint.rackAndPinion turns a wheel into a slide, joint.pulley(a, b, { over }) hangs two loads on one rope, joint.path(a, b, { path }) keeps a cart on its track, and swingTwist and sixDof make shoulders and joints of your own.

A vehicle is a body on wheels: vehicle.car(body, { wheels }), vehicle.motorcycle or vehicle.tracked, its wheels meshes placed on the body where they rest. Add it with world.physics.add and drive it with the keyboard: world.controls.vehicle = car, then world.controls.kind = 'vehicle'. Its engine, gearbox, suspension and brakes are a real machine's; car.speed, car.gear and car.rpm tell how it goes.
connect-drive-and-break.tryIt: Open the door and the drawer, then drop the stone on the bridge. Lower the bridge strength and rebuild it: it breaks under its own weight.

your-own-scene.title: Your own scene
your-own-scene.description: You now know every piece. This chapter puts them together in one small scene that you can copy and make your own.
steps: Start like chapter 1: a canvas, and createWorld with the orbit controller.
Build with shapes and materials, as in chapters 2 and 3: an island, a house, a tree and a windmill.
Light it with a sun that casts shadows (chapter 4), and move the sun with the hour.
Turn the sails in world.onFrame (chapter 6). They are four boxes in one group, so turning the group turns them all.
Open the full code, change a number, press Run: the scene is yours. Then load a model of your own (chapter 7).
your-own-scene.tryIt: Change the hour, the wind and the colour of the roof.

install.title: Install Trillion3D
install.description: Install the package, compile a model and draw it in a page: the commands, the CDN import, the supported platforms, the two server headers and the licence.
install.html:
Install

Trillion3D is not published on npm yet; the commands below work from its first release on.

You need Node.js 22.18 or newer. In your project's folder:

npm install trillion3d

This brings the engine for the browser, the Node API and the model compiler. The compiler is a native program, and npm installs only the build for your machine: macOS on Apple silicon or Intel, Linux arm64 or x64 (glibc), Windows x64. On any other machine, compiling stops with T3D-E079; the engine itself still runs in the browser.

Compile a model

The engine draws compiled models: the compiler cuts a model into small pieces that the browser streams. Put your model in public/ — glTF, GLB, OBJ, FBX or USD — then run:

npx trillion3d-compile public/model.glb public/model slice 150000 /

In order: the model, the output folder, the scope, the triangle budget, and the address at which your server shows the model's folder. The compiled model is public/model/native/slice/manifest.json.

Draw it

Save this page as public/index.html. The importmap loads the engine from a CDN: no bundler, no build step.

<!doctype html>
<canvas id="viewer" style="width: 100%; height: 90vh"></canvas>
<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "trillion3d": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/trillion3d/dist/trillion3d.module.js" } }
</script>
<script type="module">
  import { createWorld, light } from 'trillion3d';

  const world = createWorld('viewer');
  world.scene.add(light.directional({ intensity: 3, position: [5, 10, 2] }));
  world.scene.add(light.ambient({ intensity: 0.4 }));
  world.camera.position.set(3, 2, 4);
  world.camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);
  await world.scene.load('/model/native/slice/manifest.json');
</script>

Serve the public/ folder with any static web server and open its address; a page opened as a file does not work. With a bundler, import trillion3d as installed instead: the SDK guide says which files to serve beside it.

Two server headers for physics

Physics runs on several threads only in a cross-origin isolated page. Have your server send these two headers with the page:

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless

Without them everything still works: physics runs on one thread, slower with many bodies, with no error and no warning. Type crossOriginIsolated in the browser console to see which one you have. A browser that does not know credentialless needs require-corp, which asks every file from another site for a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header.

Warnings and errors

Every message of the compiler has a code and says its cause and what to do. T3D-E… is an error: nothing is written. T3D-W… is a warning: the model is compiled all the same, and --strict turns it into a failure. T3D-I… is an information, shown with --verbose.

Licence

Trillion3D is under the PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 licence. It is free for any non-commercial use: learning, personal projects, research, teaching, a charity. A commercial use needs a licence from the owner, Alban Pasquelin: ask him by opening an issue.

hlod.title: Draw far away with HLOD
hlod.description: Past the loading range, the compiler's stand-ins draw each cell of objects: four levels, from the objects batched to one simple shell per wide cell. Mark the objects, compile, draw, and check in the HLOD and triangles views.
hlod.html:
What HLOD is

A city seen from a tower holds thousands of objects past the loading range. Drawing each of them costs too many draws and too much memory; leaving them out leaves holes on the horizon. HLOD — hierarchical levels of detail — groups the objects of each cell of the ground and gives the cell stand-ins built by the compiler, each coarser and covering a wider cell than the one before. Near the camera every object is drawn itself; farther away its cell's stand-in is drawn in its place, and the view never stops at a distance.

The default chain has four levels:

  • HLOD 0: the cell's objects themselves, batched — the same meshes, drawn together past the main loading range.
  • HLOD 1, 2 and 3: one closed shell per cell, simplified to about a pixel at the distance it is first seen from, its materials baked into one texture. Each level's cells are twice as wide as the level before.

Everything is decided when the model is compiled: the page that draws it has nothing to set. See it in the example HLOD across a long district, two kilometres of street.

1. Mark the objects

The compiler builds an HLOD only over the objects it is told about. The simplest way is a mark on the glTF node, written by the tool or the code that makes the scene: buildings, foliage or props.

{
  "nodes": [
    { "name": "Tower 12", "mesh": 3, "extras": { "hlod": "buildings" } },
    { "name": "Oak 7", "mesh": 8, "extras": { "hlod": "foliage" } },
    { "name": "Bench 40", "mesh": 11, "extras": { "hlod": "props" } }
  ]
}
  • buildings: the main chain, all its levels.
  • foliage: a short chain of two levels with a voxel half as large, to keep the silhouettes of trees.
  • props: small objects, batched in cells of their own and absorbed by the main chain's first shell.

An object nothing names has no HLOD: it is streamed and drawn in its cell, and nothing stands for it farther away. Keep it that way for what moves — cars, doors, characters: an HLOD is for what stands still.

2. Compile with Node

import { prepare } from 'trillion3d';

await prepare('public/district.gltf', 'public/district', 'full', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  hlod: { levels: 4, quality: 'balanced' },
});

That is the whole option of the example: its objects are marked, so no group needs naming. Without marks, name the objects of each group — by a node's exact name, a regular expression on it, or a match on what the glTF carries (node, mesh, material, values of the node's extras; every field named must match):

await prepare('public/city.glb', 'public/city', 'slice', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  hlod: {
    levels: 4,         // 2 to 8, HLOD 0 included
    quality: 'high',   // 'low', 'balanced' or 'high'
    groups: {
      buildings: /^(House|Tower)/,
      foliage: { mesh: /tree/i },
      props: { node: /^(Lamp|Bench)/, extras: { kind: 'street' } },
    },
  },
});

A node's mark comes first; then the first group, in key order, that matches the object takes it. The quality sets every shell:

qualityDeviation allowedTexture side
'low'2 pixels512 texels
'balanced' (default)1 pixel1024 texels
'high'half a pixel2048 texels

The pixel is measured at the distance a shell is first seen from. levels defaults to 4.

3. Compile from the command line

npx trillion3d-compile '--hlod={"levels":4,"quality":"balanced"}' public/district.gltf public/district full 150000 /

The flag holds either form as JSON, anywhere on the line; a regular expression is written { "regex": "^Tree", "flags": "i" }:

npx trillion3d-compile '--hlod={"groups":{"foliage":{"mesh":{"regex":"tree","flags":"i"}}}}' public/city.glb public/city slice 150000 /

4. Compile many models at once

import { prepareMany } from 'trillion3d';

await prepareMany(
  [
    { source: 'public/district.gltf', cache: 'public/district', resourceBaseUrl: '/', hlod: { levels: 4 } },
    { source: 'public/forest.gltf', cache: 'public/forest', resourceBaseUrl: '/', hlod: { levels: 2, quality: 'low' } },
  ],
  { workers: 2 },
);

This site compiles its own example the same way: the option sits beside the code that writes the scene, and the list of scenes reads it.

// scripts/docs/examples/district.ts
export const DISTRICT_HLOD: HlodOptions = { levels: 4, quality: 'balanced' };

// scripts/site-caches.ts
'long-district': { ...example('long-district'), hlod: DISTRICT_HLOD },

5. Draw it

The page loads the compiled model as any other; the stand-ins come with it.

<!doctype html>
<canvas id="viewer" style="width: 100%; height: 90vh"></canvas>
<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "trillion3d": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/trillion3d/dist/trillion3d.module.js" } }
</script>
<script type="module">
  import { createWorld, light } from 'trillion3d';

  const world = createWorld('viewer', { controls: 'firstPerson' });
  world.camera.far = 3000;
  world.scene.add(light.directional({ intensity: 3, position: [60, 90, 40] }));
  world.scene.add(light.hemisphere({ intensity: 1.2 }));
  await world.scene.load('/district/native/full/manifest.json');
</script>

6. Check it

Choose the HLOD view (world.diagnostic.mode = 'hlod'): each pixel takes the colour of what drew it.

ColourWhat is drawn
whitethe object itself, within the main loading range
blueHLOD 0: the cell's objects, batched
yellowHLOD 1: one shell per cell
purpleHLOD 2: one shell per wider cell
cyanHLOD 3: one shell per widest cell (grey beyond, for a longer chain)

The colours alone prove nothing: switch to the coloured triangles view ('triangles'). Near, the triangles of every object; far away, a few large triangles per cell — simple boxes for whole blocks —, fewer at each level. The x-ray view shows every triangle submitted, hidden ones too: tick Freeze culling, then walk aside to see what was kept for the camera you left.

world.diagnostic.mode = 'hlod';      // white, blue, yellow, purple, cyan
world.diagnostic.mode = 'triangles'; // simple shells far away
world.diagnostic.mode = 'xray';      // every triangle submitted, hidden ones too
world.diagnostic.freeze = true;      // hold the cut, then step aside

The expert form

For full control: named layers, each with its builder and the layer above it (parent), and rules that assign objects to the instanced layers. The simple form stands for exactly such a list; the two forms cannot be mixed.

hlod: {
  layers: [
    { name: 'buildings', builder: 'instanced', parent: 'city1' },
    { name: 'city1', builder: 'approximate', parent: 'city2', deviationPixels: 1 },
    { name: 'city2', builder: 'approximate', textureSize: 2048 },
    { name: 'trees', builder: 'instanced', parent: 'canopy' },
    { name: 'canopy', builder: 'approximate', accuracyPixels: 0.3 },
  ],
  assign: [{ match: { node: /^Tree/, extras: { kind: 'tree' } }, layer: 'trees' }],
  default: 'buildings',
}
  • Builders: instanced, the objects themselves (objects are assigned to these layers); approximate, one closed shell per cell, its materials baked; merge, the cell's objects merged into one mesh; proxy, the cell's objects remeshed into one closed surface.
  • Settings, in metres or in pixels, never both: accuracy or accuracyPixels the voxel, deviation or deviationPixels the deviation allowed, textureSize the texture side, a power of two from 16 to 8192.
  • Each rule, and default, names an instanced layer; the first rule that matches wins. A node's extras.hlod mark names a layer by its name here.

Pitfalls

  • No HLOD appears: the job names none, or no object is marked or matched — a job whose HLOD takes no object is refused.
  • A mark naming no group nor layer, a mark in a job without hlod, an unknown field, quality or group: the job is refused, in the words you wrote.
  • Something moves and leaves a ghost far away: it was given a group. Leave moving objects unnamed.
  • The far shells look too coarse: raise quality to 'high' rather than adding levels; more levels reach farther, not finer.

In depth: docs/COMPILER.md. The anti-aliasing options are set in the same call: Temporal anti-aliasing.

temporal-antialiasing.title: Temporal anti-aliasing
temporal-antialiasing.description: Smooth edges and steady fine detail: the level for the whole scene, who decides between the scene, the quality, the page and the editor, and how much history each material may keep.
temporal-antialiasing.html:
What it does

A pixel samples one point of the scene: thin wires, edges and fine textures then show stairs and shimmer. The temporal anti-aliasing shifts the camera by a fraction of a pixel at every image and blends each new image into a history of the images before, moved along with the surfaces. Over a few images every pixel gathers many samples: smooth edges, steady fine detail, at the cost of one image.

It is set at two scales: for the whole scene (a level, from off to the finest), and for each material (how much history its pixels may keep). See it in Smooth edges over time and Responsive particles.

For the whole scene

The level is written in the compiled scene, so it travels with it: 'off', 'low', 'medium', 'high' or 'max', from the cheapest to the finest. true stands for the default level, false for 'off'.

import { prepare } from 'trillion3d';

await prepare('public/street.glb', 'public/street', 'full', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  temporalAntialiasing: 'high',
});
npx trillion3d-compile --temporal-antialiasing=high public/street.glb public/street full 150000 /

In a batch, each job has its own field:

{
  "jobs": [
    { "source": "public/street.glb", "cache": "public/street", "resourceBaseUrl": "/", "temporalAntialiasing": "high" },
    { "source": "public/plan.glb", "cache": "public/plan", "resourceBaseUrl": "/", "temporalAntialiasing": "off" }
  ]
}

The page can still decide, at creation or at any moment:

const world = createWorld('viewer', { temporalAntialiasing: 'medium' });
await world.scene.load('/street/native/full/manifest.json');

world.temporalAntialiasing = 'off';  // switched live, next image
world.temporalAntialiasing = true;   // back to the default level

Who decides, from the strongest to the weakest:

RankWhoHow
1the scene editorits own setting
2the pagecreateWorld(…, { temporalAntialiasing }), world.temporalAntialiasing = …
3the quality levelthe quality the world runs at
4the compiled scenetemporalAntialiasing, --temporal-antialiasing=
5the defaultnothing named

With several scenes in one world, the first scene loaded that names a level decides for the scene rank.

For each material

Each material holds one number from 0 to 1: the share of history the anti-aliasing may keep on its pixels. 1 is the full smoothing; 0 shows its pixels from the current image alone. Four presets name the usual values:

PresetHistory keptFor
'normal'1everything, by default
'responsive'0.75small fast effects: sparks, embers, blinking lights
'soft'0.5surfaces that change a lot from one image to the next: screens, animated textures
'off'0pixels that must stay exactly as drawn: text, a user interface in the scene

Any number between is allowed. Set it by material name at compile time, or in the glTF material itself:

await prepare('public/arcade.glb', 'public/arcade', 'full', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  materials: {
    'screen': { temporalAntialiasing: 'soft' },
    'score text': { temporalAntialiasing: 'off' },
    'neon': { temporalAntialiasing: 0.6 },
  },
});
npx trillion3d-compile '--materials={"screen":{"temporalAntialiasing":"soft"}}' public/arcade.glb public/arcade full 150000 /
{ "name": "score text", "extras": { "temporalAntialiasing": "off" } }

responsive is a shortcut for 0.75 — the current image then weighs exactly a quarter: see Responsive anti-aliasing. When several settings name one material, the first of this list wins:

  1. materials: { name: { temporalAntialiasing } };
  2. materials: { name: { responsive: true } };
  3. the responsive option matching its object;
  4. "extras": { "temporalAntialiasing": … } in the glTF;
  5. "extras": { "responsive": true } in the glTF;
  6. otherwise 1.

See it

The TAA history by material view (world.diagnostic.mode = 'taa-material-history') shows each pixel's material value as grey: white 1, black 0. Compare with the no temporal AA view, the raw image of the frame, and the frame difference view, which lights whatever changed since the image before — a still view that keeps lighting up shimmers.

world.diagnostic.mode = 'taa-material-history'; // white 1, black 0
world.diagnostic.mode = 'no-temporal-aa';       // the raw image of this frame
world.diagnostic.mode = 'frame-difference';     // what changed since the last image

Pitfalls

  • 'off' on a material is sharper, but its edges then follow the camera's sub-pixel shift: they may shimmer, even when nothing moves. Keep it for text and flat interfaces.
  • A trail behind a fast object with good motion — a car, a character — is not a case for a lower value: the history follows them. Lower values are for what the engine cannot follow.
  • Turning the whole scene 'off' to fix one material costs the smoothing everywhere: set that material instead.
  • A material name is matched exactly, as written in the glTF.

The same call compiles the HLOD: Draw far away with HLOD.

responsive-antialiasing.title: Responsive anti-aliasing for fast effects
responsive-antialiasing.description: On a responsive material the current image weighs exactly a quarter, so small fast effects such as sparks leave no trail. Three ways to ask for it when compiling, which one wins, and the view that shows it.
responsive-antialiasing.html:
What it does

The temporal anti-aliasing blends each new image into a history of the images before, moved along with the surfaces (Temporal anti-aliasing). It works where the engine knows how each pixel moved. A small bright spark crossing many pixels in one image, a blinking light, an effect animated in its shader: the history cannot follow them, and they leave a trail behind them or fade.

A responsive material changes one thing: on its pixels the blend takes exactly a quarter of each new image (1/4) — it keeps 0.75 of its history —, so their history catches up within a few images. Everything else keeps the full smoothing.

When to use it

  • Yes: sparks, embers, small fast particles, blinking lights — small effects that change faster than the history can follow.
  • No: ordinary objects, even fast ones — a car, a character, a turning wheel. The engine knows their motion, the history follows them, and responsive pixels would only shimmer more.

The example Responsive particles shows the difference: two swarms of sparks with the same motion; the left one is responsive, its trails short; the right one is not.

Three ways to ask for it

The flag is set when the scene is compiled; the page changes nothing. The example's left swarm uses all three, one colour each: orange (A), cyan (B), pink (C).

A — responsive: match the objects

One match, as an HLOD group names its objects: a node's exact name, a regular expression on it, or { node, mesh, material, extras }. The materials of every object it matches become responsive; a match naming material keeps only those materials.

import { prepare } from 'trillion3d';

await prepare('public/sparks.gltf', 'public/sparks', 'full', 150000, {
  resourceBaseUrl: '/',
  responsive: { material: /^spark pattern$/ },
});

Other matches:

responsive: 'Fireworks',                       // the node named exactly Fireworks
responsive: /^Spark/,                          // every node whose name starts with Spark
responsive: { mesh: /ember/i },                // every node wearing an ember mesh
responsive: { extras: { effect: 'particles' } } // every node whose extras say so

B — materials: set a material by its name

materials: {
  'spark listed': { responsive: true },
  'still listed': { responsive: false },
  'still extras': { responsive: false },
},

An explicit value, false included, that wins over the two other ways.

C — the material's own glTF extras

{ "name": "spark extras", "extras": { "responsive": true } }

Written by whoever exports the model; no compile option needed.

Which one wins

RankWayWritten
1Bmaterials: { name: { responsive } }, false included
2Aresponsive: …
3C"extras": { "responsive": true }
4—otherwise not responsive

In the example, still extras asks for it in its extras, but materials sets it to false: it stays plain. A material's own temporalAntialiasing value, when one is named, comes before all three (Temporal anti-aliasing).

From the command line, in a batch, in this site

npx trillion3d-compile '--responsive={"material":{"regex":"^spark pattern$"}}' '--materials={"spark listed":{"responsive":true}}' public/sparks.gltf public/sparks full 150000 /
{
  "jobs": [
    {
      "source": "public/sparks.gltf",
      "cache": "public/sparks",
      "resourceBaseUrl": "/",
      "responsive": { "material": { "regex": "^spark pattern$" } },
      "materials": { "spark listed": { "responsive": true } }
    }
  ]
}

Each flag holds JSON; a regular expression is written { "regex": "^spark", "flags": "i" }. This site declares its example's options beside the code that writes the sparks:

// scripts/docs/examples/sparks.ts
export const SPARKS_RESPONSIVE: ResponsiveOption = { material: /^spark pattern$/ };
export const SPARKS_MATERIALS: MaterialsOption = {
  'spark listed': { responsive: true },
  'still listed': { responsive: false },
  'still extras': { responsive: false },
};

// scripts/site-caches.ts
'particles-responsive': {
  ...example('particles-responsive'),
  responsive: SPARKS_RESPONSIVE,
  materials: SPARKS_MATERIALS,
},

Draw it

<!doctype html>
<canvas id="viewer" style="width: 100%; height: 90vh"></canvas>
<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "trillion3d": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/trillion3d/dist/trillion3d.module.js" } }
</script>
<script type="module">
  import { createWorld, light } from 'trillion3d';

  const world = createWorld('viewer', { controls: 'orbit', temporalAntialiasing: true });
  world.scene.add(light.directional({ intensity: 3, position: [60, 90, 40] }));
  world.scene.add(light.hemisphere({ intensity: 1.2 }));
  await world.scene.load('/sparks/native/full/manifest.json');
</script>

See it

Choose the TAA responsive view: the responsive pixels show in white. Turn the smoothing off and on again to compare the two swarms' trails; the frame difference view lights whatever changed since the image before.

world.diagnostic.mode = 'taa-responsive';   // responsive pixels in white
world.diagnostic.mode = 'frame-difference'; // what changed since the last image

Pitfalls

  • Nothing turns white: the material name in materials must be written exactly as in the glTF, and a match naming material keeps only those materials.
  • A responsive surface shimmers a little more than the others: that is the price of following fast changes. Keep it for small effects.
  • Still a trail: lower the material's own value further, 'soft' or a number (Temporal anti-aliasing).

In depth: docs/COMPILER.md.

shadow-overflows.title: Shadow and light-grid overflows
shadow-overflows.description: When too many lights or shadows crowd one pixel or one cell, the engine keeps what fits and drops the rest. Read the overflows in the frame metrics, silence the messages, and raise the capacity.
shadow-overflows.html:
What it does

Shadows and the light grid have a fixed room. When a scene asks for more than they hold — too many shadowed lights on one pixel, a full page pool, a cell with more lights than entries —, the engine does not stop: it keeps what fits and drops the rest, so a shadow or a light goes missing. Two readings tell you it happened, and two settings change the room.

Shadow overflows

In world.onFrame, metrics.shadowVsmOverflowFlags holds the kinds of overflow seen in the last 10 seconds, one bit each. It is null when there are no shadow maps.

BitKindWhat happens
1marking job queuenever set by this engine today
2one-pass projection: more shadowed local lights on a pixel than shadowOnePassProjectionMaxLightsPerPixelthe extra lights fall back to one sample of their own map
4page pool fullshadows go missing
8casters' list fullshadows go missing

shadowAllowScreenOverflowMessages is true by default; false makes the metric report 0. Each kind is still logged once in the console, whatever the option.

Light grid capacity

The view's light grid holds lightGridMaxCulledLightsPerCell light entries per cell on average (32 by default, from 1 to 1024, set through world.hiz): a fixed pool of cells × that number.

When a column finds the pool full, it keeps the lights it got, in order, and drops the rest: those lights neither light nor shadow there. metrics.tileLightPoolOverflowed says so; it is sampled one frame in fifteen.

Read them, silence them, raise the room

import { createWorld } from 'trillion3d'

const world = createWorld('viewer')

// Shadows: the overflows of the last 10 seconds
// (shadowAllowScreenOverflowMessages, true by default)
world.onFrame(({ metrics }) => {
  const seen = metrics.shadowVsmOverflowFlags // null without shadow maps
  if (seen & 2) warn('Too many shadowed lights on a pixel:'
    + ' raise shadowOnePassProjectionMaxLightsPerPixel')
  if (seen & 4) warn('Page pool full: shadows are missing')
  if (seen & 8) warn('Shadow casters list full')
})
world.shadows = { shadowAllowScreenOverflowMessages: false } // the metric reads 0
// (each kind is still logged once in the console)

// Light grid: 32 entries a cell by default
world.hiz = { lightGridMaxCulledLightsPerCell: 64 }
world.onFrame(({ metrics }) => {
  if (metrics.tileLightPoolOverflowed) warn('Light grid full:'
    + ' some lights are ignored')
})

A write names the settings it changes; null puts one back to its default.

The settings

SettingDefaultRangeWhat it does
shadowOnePassProjectionMaxLightsPerPixel161 to 32the most shadowed local lights a pixel keeps in its mask (world.shadows)
shadowAllowScreenOverflowMessagestruetrue / falsefalse makes shadowVsmOverflowFlags report 0 (world.shadows)
lightGridMaxCulledLightsPerCell321 to 1024light entries per cell, on average (world.hiz)

Pitfalls

  • Raising lightGridMaxCulledLightsPerCell costs memory: cells × entries × 4 bytes. Raise it only when tileLightPoolOverflowed turns true.
  • The per-pixel lights cap also sets the mask format: 32 bits up to 8 lights, 64 up to 16, 128 up to 32. Going past 8 or 16 lights widens the mask of every pixel.
  • Silencing the messages hides the report, not the overflow: the missing shadows stay missing.
  • tileLightPoolOverflowed is sampled one frame in fifteen: a very short overflow can pass between two samples.

Reference: ShadowOptions, ShadowFrameMetrics, world.hiz.

contact-shadows.title: Contact shadows
contact-shadows.description: A short ray from each pixel toward each light finds what touches a surface, where a shadow map is too coarse. Set its length on a light, override it for the whole view, or switch it off.
contact-shadows.html:
What it does

A shadow map is too coarse for what stands against a surface: a book on a shelf, a cup on a table. The lit passes add a contact shadow of their own: a short ray from each pixel toward each light, through the depth of the scene, eight steps long, which darkens the pixel where something touches it in the light's way.

Every light's ray is 0 long by default, and only a light that casts a shadow (castShadow) casts one: a scene draws no contact shadow until a light asks for it.

On a light

Each light names its own, as properties, as parameters of the light tool and as fields of a saved scene. Every kind of light has them.

PropertyDefaultRangeWhat it does
contactShadowLength0from 0the ray's length; 0 casts none (screen units unless the next)
contactShadowLengthInWorldSpacefalsetrue / falsethe length is in metres
contactShadowCastingIntensity10 to 1how dark the shadow is where the ray meets a surface that casts contact shadows
contactShadowNonCastingIntensity00 to 1how dark it is where it meets one that does not (an eye's)
indirectLightingIntensity1from 0the factor on the light it gives the scene's indirect lighting

A light that casts no shadow gives the material's occlusion to its lobes: a pixel in a crease of an ambient-occlusion map is darker under it, as the shadow of a light that casts one already is.

On the view

The view's settings are shadow settings: options of createWorld, and world.shadows changes them from the next frame. No quality level writes them.

View optionDefaultRangeWhat it does
contactShadowstruetrue / falsewhether the lights cast their rays; off, none do
contactShadowOverrideLength-1any numberreplaces every light's length when it is 0 or more; below 0, the lights' own
contactShadowOverrideLengthInWorldSpacefalsetrue / falsewhether that length is in metres
contactShadowOverrideCastingIntensity-1-1 to 1replaces every light's casting intensity when it is 0 or more
contactShadowOverrideNonCastingIntensity-1-1 to 1replaces every light's non-casting intensity when it is 0 or more
contactShadowMethod00 / 1how the lights' rays are cast: 0 the short ray every lit pixel casts, 1 the Bend screen-space shadow, a texture of the light's own made before the lighting
contactShadowBendSurfaceThickness0.0050.00001 to 1how thick the surface a pixel stands for is taken to be when a Bend ray meets it (a share of the depth left to the far plane); method 1 only
contactShadowBendMaxLights81 to 16how many lights Bend serves in an image, the suns first then the local lights nearest the eye; the others cast the short ray; each costs a texture of the image's size (4 bytes a pixel)
contactShadowIntensityMode00 to 2how the Bend shadow's intensity is found: 0 by the hit surface's castContactShadow, 1 by its depth, from the non-casting intensity to the casting one over a fade, 2 the casting intensity everywhere
contactShadowIntensityFadeStart1600from 0the depth, in centimetres, where that fade begins; read in mode 1
contactShadowIntensityFadeLength800from 0.0001the length of that fade, in centimetres; read in mode 1

With contactShadowMethod at 1, up to contactShadowBendMaxLights lights cast the Bend screen-space shadow in place of the short ray: a wavefront marched from each pixel toward the light, into a texture of the light's own made before the lighting. The options after it are read only then.

Use them

// A lamp whose shadow holds the books down on the shelf: a ray of a fiftieth of the screen's height, on a light that casts.
const lamp = light.point({ intensity: 20, position: [0, 3, 0], distance: 12, castShadow: true })
lamp.contactShadowLength = 0.02
// A sun with its ray in metres, and a shadow half as dark.
const sun = light.directional({ castShadow: true, contactShadowLength: 0.3, contactShadowLengthInWorldSpace: true, contactShadowCastingIntensity: 0.5 })
// The view: every light's ray at four hundredths of the screen's height, then back to the lights' own; or none at all.
const world = createWorld('viewer', { contactShadowOverrideLength: 0.04 })
world.shadows = { contactShadowOverrideLength: null }
world.shadows = { contactShadows: false }

A write names the settings it changes; null puts one back to its default.

Pitfalls

  • Nothing appears: the light must cast a shadow (castShadow) and have a length above 0, its own or the view's override, and the view's contactShadows must be on.
  • The eye and hair shading models cast a ray whatever the light and the switch say: a pixel of the eye model casts half a centimetre toward every light, one of the hair model a fifth of the half height of the screen at its depth under a light that casts no shadow. The override length does not move them.
  • In screen units the ray follows the depth of the pixel: about 0.01 is a sharp contact. Use contactShadowLengthInWorldSpace for a length in metres.
  • indirectLightingIntensity sits on the same record but is not a shadow: it is the factor on the light the light gives the scene's indirect lighting (1 by default, from 0).

Reference: Light, LIGHT_CONTACT_SHADOW_RULES, ShadowOptions, world.shadows.

shadow-compute-throttle.title: Throttle the shadow maps' compute
shadow-compute-throttle.description: When the shadow raster costs too much, the dynamic resolution can lower the maps' resolution, wholly on the GPU. Off by default: name a load budget or a time budget to turn it on.
shadow-compute-throttle.html:
What it does

Beside the page pool's bias (shadowDynamicResolutionMaxResolutionLodBias), the dynamic resolution can lower the resolution of the shadow maps when the shadow raster costs too much. It works wholly on the GPU: the raster counts the clusters it draws in each map, and the next frame's two kernels carry the counts to the maps and add to each map's bias the share of the cost it takes. Nothing is read back.

It is off while shadowDynamicResolutionTimeBudgetMs and shadowDynamicResolutionLoadBudget are both 0, the default: nothing is counted, made or run.

Two budgets

shadowDynamicResolutionLoadBudget is the estimated load of the raster past which the bias rises; lower is more aggressive.

shadowDynamicResolutionTimeBudgetMs fits the raster's GPU time to a number of milliseconds through the render scale's heuristic. It needs the render scale on 'auto' and a GPU timer, and it wins when both budgets are named.

Shape the throttle

shadowDynamicResolutionPerVsmBiasHistoryWeight eases each map over the frames: the share of its bias that the frame before keeps.

shadowDynamicResolutionMaxComputeResolutionLodBiasDirectional and shadowDynamicResolutionMaxComputeResolutionLodBiasLocal cap what a sun's maps and a local light's maps may take, within shadowDynamicResolutionMaxResolutionLodBias less the pool's bias.

Use them

world.shadows = { shadowDynamicResolutionLoadBudget: 1 } // throttle the maps when the raster's load passes 1
world.shadows = { shadowDynamicResolutionTimeBudgetMs: 3 } // fit the raster to 3 ms (render scale 'auto')
world.shadows = { shadowDynamicResolutionMaxComputeResolutionLodBiasLocal: 1 } // local lights lose one level at most
world.shadows = { shadowDynamicResolutionPerVsmBiasHistoryWeight: 0.5 } // ease faster
world.shadows = { shadowDynamicResolutionLoadBudget: null } // back to the default: off

A write names the settings it changes; null puts one back to its default.

The settings

SettingDefaultRangeWhat it does
shadowDynamicResolutionTimeBudgetMs0 (off)from 0the GPU milliseconds the shadow raster may take; 0 is off
shadowDynamicResolutionLoadBudget0 (off)from 0the raster's estimated load past which the maps lose resolution; 0 is off
shadowDynamicResolutionPerVsmBiasHistoryWeight0.90 to 1the share of a map's bias that the frame before keeps
shadowDynamicResolutionMaxComputeResolutionLodBiasDirectional99999from 0the most levels it adds to a sun's maps
shadowDynamicResolutionMaxComputeResolutionLodBiasLocal99999from 0the most levels it adds to a point, spot or rectangle light's maps

Pitfalls

  • Turning a budget on or off makes no shadow set again: the page pool and the cache stay as they are.
  • The two budgets do not add up: when both are named, the time budget wins and the load budget is ignored.
  • A lower resolution makes softer shadows: raise the budget, or cap the levels, when a shadow loses too much.

Reference: ShadowOptions, world.shadows.

canvas-size-and-pixel-error.title: Canvas size and the cut's pixel error
canvas-size-and-pixel-error.description: How the drawing buffer follows the canvas, how to resize it, and how the cut's pixel error trades detail for speed.
canvas-size-and-pixel-error.html:
The drawing buffer follows the canvas's CSS box, and pixelRatio the browser's, unless set; world.resize(width, height) sets a size, omitted arguments reading the CSS box. A canvas hidden or zero-size at creation needs an explicit resize() or showing first; one hidden later keeps its last size.

world.pixelError is the DAG cut's screen error in pixels (1 by default: a coarser level strays at most one pixel from the finer one; 0 keeps the exact leaves, a larger value selects coarser pages when the cache has them). pose.fromBounds(box) frames a box, pose.pointOfInterest(name, pose) names one, pose.runPath(world, poses, { images }) replays a path, one display frame per pose, and answers the frames drawn, their CPU time summarized and the display cadence.

Reference: world.pixelError.

software-raster.title: Software raster
software-raster.description: Draw the smallest triangles in compute instead of the device's rasterizer: the options that choose which clusters go there.
software-raster.html:
world.softwareRaster (option of createWorld too, true by default) rasters in compute each cluster whose longest edge projects under world.hardwareRasterEdgePixels (option of createWorld too, 32 by default, a finite number of pixels above zero) and whose box crosses neither clip plane; every other cluster goes to the hardware rasterizer, and false hands it every one. world.depthBucketing (option of createWorld too, true by default, the reference's) rasters the software raster's cutout clusters nearest first, so that a hidden cutout pixel leaves before its texture is read: each cluster is put in one of 256 buckets spread by the logarithm of the view depth of its box between world.depthBucketsMinZ (10) and world.depthBucketsMaxZ (1000), in metres, finite numbers above zero (the reference's centimetres, 1000 and 100000). As in the reference, the order is made only where the scene holds voxels; it never changes a pixel. All five are render settings: the page's value holds over the quality preset, a write applies next frame, and a value of another kind is refused by name.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { softwareRaster: true, hardwareRasterEdgePixels: 32 })
world.softwareRaster = false // every cluster on the hardware rasterizer, from the next frame
world.hardwareRasterEdgePixels = 16 // fewer clusters on the software raster
world.depthBucketing = false // the cutout clusters unordered
world.depthBucketsMaxZ = 500 // the buckets end at 500 m

Reference: world.softwareRaster, world.hardwareRasterEdgePixels, world.depthBucketing, world.depthBucketsMinZ, world.depthBucketsMaxZ.

cut-settings.title: The cut's settings
cut-settings.description: The settings of the cut, the choice of which pages and clusters to draw: two-pass occlusion and the options beside it.
cut-settings.html:
world.cut holds the cut's settings, each an option of createWorld too: cutTwoPassOcclusion (true: the main view tests what it cuts against the previous image's depth, then what that hid against the depth it just drew), cutOcclusionCulling, cutFrustumCulling and cutMinLodCulling (true: each test on), cutDrawDistanceCulling (true: an object that names a draw distance — drawDistance — is culled outside it, in the cut, in the sun's shadows and in the rays' scene; false, every instance of an instanced mesh is drawn at every distance, while an object of its own is always culled by its distances), cutDistanceCullToSphereEdge (true: an object's draw distance is measured to the edge of the sphere of its bounds; false, to its centre), cutViewDistanceScale (1, a finite number of at least 0: the scale every draw distance is multiplied by; the quality levels write it, 0.4 at smooth, 0.6 at balanced, 0.8 at fine, 1 at max, 10 at cinematic), cutViewDistanceApplySecondaryScale (false) and cutViewDistanceSecondaryScale (1): a second scale of the draw distances, applied beside the first once the switch is on, cutViewDistanceFovMinAngle (45) and cutViewDistanceFovMaxAngle (90), two horizontal fields of view in degrees from 0 to 360, with cutViewDistanceFovMinAngleScale and cutViewDistanceFovMaxAngleScale (1 both, 0 or more): the scale the draw distances of an object of its own take at the first angle and under, at the second and over, and linearly between (an orthographic view counts as 0 degrees; at 1 and 1 nothing changes), cutEdgeScaleBudgetMs (0, none) and cutEdgeScaleMinPercent (30): a GPU time budget for the main view's cut and its raster that coarsens its threshold, no further than that share of its scale, while the render scale is 'auto', cutLodBiasFollowsUpscale (true: an upscaled image's screen error follows the display over the render width), cutLodBiasOffset (0) and cutLodBiasMin (-2), that bias's offset and floor in powers of two, and the caps of its lists, cutMaxNodes (2097152), cutMaxCandidateClusters (16777216) and cutMaxVisibleClusters (4194304): past one, the cut draws what fits and warns. Of these only cutViewDistanceScale is written by a quality level: a value the page set holds over the preset. A write names the settings it changes, null one's default; a value of another kind is refused by name.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { cutTwoPassOcclusion: true })
world.cut = { cutLodBiasFollowsUpscale: false } // the screen error ignores the upscale, next frame
world.cut = { cutViewDistanceScale: 0.5 } // every object's draw distance halved
world.cut = { cutViewDistanceFovMaxAngleScale: 0.5 } // an object of its own: halved at 90 degrees and over
world.cut = { cutEdgeScaleBudgetMs: 6 } // with renderScale 'auto': the cut coarsens above 6 ms

Reference: world.cut.

depth-pyramid-and-occlusion.title: Depth pyramid and occlusion culling
depth-pyramid-and-occlusion.description: The depth pyramid's settings, the light grid view, and the occlusion tests that leave out what the depth hides.
depth-pyramid-and-occlusion.html:
world.hiz holds the depth pyramid's settings, each an option of createWorld too: hizTrace ('reference': the reflections' trace walks the closest opaque depth of each half-resolution texel, mip by mip, down to the full-resolution depth, as the reference's does; 'planes': it reads each pixel as a plane, which keeps a hit on a grazing surface that the centre alone passes over), hizFoldTransparents (false: the trace layers hold the opaque depth alone; true, the nearest transparent surface of each pixel too, so a ray stops at glass) and hizTransparentTest ('finer': a transparent cluster is tested over up to sixteen texels a side of a fine level; 'reference': over four texels a side of the lowest level that holds it; the image is the same, 'finer' rejects more clusters), hizFullResDepth (true: the screen probes' 'reference' walk goes down to the full-resolution depth; false stops at the half-resolution level, a little less exact and cheaper; the reflections' walk always goes down) and lightGridHizCull (true: the light grid leaves empty the cells behind the farthest depth of their column of the image, read from the pyramid the image built; false lists every cell the lights reach), lightGridLinkedLists (true: the cells' lists are chains of links taken from one pool shared by the whole grid, and when links run short each cell keeps the first lights of its list; false: each cell has its own lightGridMaxCulledLightsPerCell words and keeps its first lights up to them) and lightGridMaxCulledLightsPerCell (32: the light entries the view's light grid holds per cell, from 1 to 1024; the pool holds that many for each cell; the lights asked past it are dropped, with one console warning). The cut's occlusion reads the culling layer, which no setting changes. A write names the settings it changes, null one's default; a value of another kind is refused by name.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { hizTrace: 'planes' })
world.hiz = { hizTrace: null, hizFoldTransparents: true } // the default trace, glass in the pyramid
world.hiz = { hizFullResDepth: false, lightGridHizCull: false } // half-resolution probe walk, no cull
world.hiz = { lightGridLinkedLists: false, lightGridMaxCulledLightsPerCell: 64 } // 64 words of its own a cell

lightGridDebug (0, off) draws the light grid over the image: 1 colours each cell from blue (no light) to red (lightGridDebugMaxThreshold lights, 8 by default, from 1 to 1024) by the number of lights in the cell of each pixel's depth, 2 by the greatest number over the slices of its column but the last (the last slice's culling is too wide to mean much), 3 over all of them; the count is written in the middle of each cell and the borders are drawn in grey. lightGridDebugSlice (-1) above -1 shows the one slice of that index (read no higher than the last) whatever the view. It needs lit lights in the scene.

world.hiz = { lightGridDebug: 1 } // the lights in the cell of each pixel
world.hiz = { lightGridDebug: 3, lightGridDebugMaxThreshold: 16 } // the greatest count of a column, red at 16
world.hiz = { lightGridDebug: 1, lightGridDebugSlice: 12 } // only the twelfth slice

hizPrime ('off') builds, before a view's cut tests anything, a primed pyramid from a small, coarse draw of the objects that set farField (object.farField = true, false by default; a saved scene keeps it when true), for the cut's main pass to test against: 'whenMissing' for an image whose view has no pyramid of the image before (its first, one after a resize, one after a cut of the camera), 'always' for every image. The draw is the image's size shifted right by 1 + hizPrimeSizeBias (2: an eighth), its depth pushed away from the eye by hizPrimeDepthBias metres (1.5), its clusters cut at hizPrimeErrorScale (32) times the image's pixel error; hizPrimeFarFieldOnly (true) draws the flagged objects alone, false the whole cut. With no object flagged it draws nothing and costs nothing. The image is the same: the primed pyramid only lets the main pass skip what it hides, and the post pass judges again what it hid.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { hizPrime: 'whenMissing' })
mountains.farField = true // this object is drawn into the primed pyramid
world.hiz = { hizPrime: 'always', hizPrimeDepthBias: 3 } // every image, pushed away by 3 metres
world.hiz = { hizPrime: null } // back to the default, 'off'

hzbOcclusion (0) makes the main view leave out the objects the depth it drew hides. At 1 (or 2, forced) the world box of every object is projected each image and walked against the farthest depth of the pyramid, with the walk the transparent clusters are tested with under hizTransparentTest: 'reference' (the lowest level that holds the box in four texels a side); the verdicts are copied for the CPU and come back a few images late, and an object found behind the depth is left out of the next images' cut, in front again when a test finds it so. An object with no box, outside the view or within hzbOcclusionNeverTestDistance metres (0) of the eye is never rejected, and the shadow maps never see the verdict. hzbOcclusionExpandAmount (0) metres and hzbOcclusionExpandScreenSpace (0) pixels grow every tested box, which hides fewer objects and shows fewer of them late; hzbOcclusionExpandNewlyAmount and hzbOcclusionExpandNewlyScreenSpace (0) grow, beside them, an object not tested for hzbOcclusionFramesNotTestedToExpand (5) images for the next hzbOcclusionFramesToExpandNewly (2) images it is tested in.

occlusionQueries (off) asks the same of the GPU's own occlusion queries instead, while hzbOcclusion is 0: the world boxes of the objects are drawn sixteen to a query against the depth the image drew (depth tested, nothing written), the counts come back a few images late, and an object whose group let no sample through is left out of the next images' cut until a later group lets one through. An object with no box, or a box that reaches the eye's plane, is never hidden; at most 65536 objects are queried.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { occlusionQueries: true })
world.hiz = { occlusionQueries: null } // back to the default, off

downsampledOcclusionQueries (off) makes those queries test against a smaller copy of the depth: the image's depth is reduced to half its size on each side first, each texel keeping the farthest of the four it covers, and the boxes are drawn at that size. An object is then hidden only where the whole square of texels hides it: fewer objects are hidden and the queries count fewer samples.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { occlusionQueries: true, downsampledOcclusionQueries: true })
world.hiz = { downsampledOcclusionQueries: null } // back to the default, off
const world = createWorld('viewer', { hzbOcclusion: 1 })
world.hiz = { hzbOcclusionExpandScreenSpace: 8, hzbOcclusionNeverTestDistance: 2 } // grown by 8 pixels, none tested within 2 m
world.hiz = { hzbOcclusion: null } // back to the default, none

Reference: world.hiz.

tessellation.title: Run-time tessellation
tessellation.description: Run-time tessellation: its settings, its capacities, and what it does not do.
tessellation.html:
world.tessellation holds the settings of the run-time tessellation, each an option of createWorld too. A write names the settings it changes, null one's default; a value of another kind is refused by name. They are render settings: the page's value holds over the quality preset (no preset level writes them), and a write applies next frame.

SettingTakesDefault
tessellationtrue / false: displaced materials are tessellated and displaced; false draws every one flat and runs nothing of the tessellationtrue
tessellationDicingRateA finite number of pixels above 0: the size a micro-triangle is diced to; smaller cuts finer and costs more2
tessellationMaxPatchesPerGroupA whole number of at least 1: the patches one group of the dicing takes (held to 21)5
tessellationMaxCandidatePatchesA whole number from 1 to 134217727: the patches the splitting queue holds, 16 bytes each2097152
tessellationMaxVisiblePatchesA whole number from 1 to 134217727: the patches a pass's visible list holds, 16 bytes each2097152
tessellationShadowsDirectionaltrue / false: the shadow maps of the suns take a displaced surface's displaced shapetrue
tessellationShadowsLocaltrue / false: the shadow maps of the local lights (points and spots) take ittrue

A patch past either capacity is lost for the image. The buffers hold what the device lets one storage buffer bind: capacities that would not fit are brought down in proportion. Neither shadow setting does anything while tessellation is off or the scene holds no displaced material.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { tessellationDicingRate: 2 })
world.tessellation = { tessellationDicingRate: 4 } // coarser micro-triangles, from the next frame
world.tessellation = { tessellationShadowsLocal: false } // lamps cast the flat surface
world.tessellation = { tessellation: false } // every displaced material drawn flat
world.tessellation = { tessellation: null, tessellationDicingRate: null } // back to the defaults

The explorer's tool trillion3d_set_tessellation writes one setting at a time (field, value). Nothing of the tessellation is allocated while the setting is off or no displaced material is in the scene; turning it off gives the buffers back.

What tessellation does not do:

  • A displaced surface is drawn flat by the passes that do not read the visibility buffer's pixels: the rays' scene and the reflections' traced scene see the surface its triangles describe. Its motion vector is the flat surface's point moved as the surface moves, plus this image's displacement, whole: the displacement itself is not tracked from image to image, so a height map that changes in time gets no velocity from its change.
  • A masked displaced surface casts a tessellated shadow, cut out at the vertices of its patches on a device that grants nine storage buffers to a vertex stage and per pixel on a device that grants eight, which every WebGPU device does. A shadow patch is judged by the frustum of the map and the page it casts into, not by the depth the page has already seen.
  • A per-job override of a material's displacement fields is not read. The displacement baked into a mesh is read for the rigid triangle primitives of a mesh, tessellated together; a primitive that deforms, or stands for a part of an assembly, bakes none.
  • A scene compiled before the texture-coordinate density existed reads a density of 1 for every set; recompile it to measure it.

Reference: world.tessellation.

volumetric-lightmap.title: Volumetric lightmap
volumetric-lightmap.description: The precomputed indirect light a baked scene carries, and the option that turns its reading on or off.
volumetric-lightmap.html:
world.volumetricLightmap holds the setting of the precomputed indirect light a baked scene carries (a volumetric-lightmap.bin), an option of createWorld too: volumetricLightmap (true: the lightmap is read by the fog's static term and by the lighting of movable objects; false: every read of it answers black, as in a scene without one; it does nothing where the scene has no lightmap), volumetricLightmapLoadingRange (64: the metres around the view within which the cells of the finest bricks are loaded) and volumetricLightmapBrickMemory (30: the megabytes of finest bricks that stay resident, the cells nearest the view winning them). The fog's static term is scaled by the heightFog part's volumetric.staticLightingScatteringIntensity (1, never below 0; 0 leaves the term out). The fog's sky light follows the sky light part's mobility: a 'static' one lights the fog by none of its own harmonics (its light is the lightmap's), a 'stationary' one that casts shadows scatters multiplied by the lightmap's sky visibility (a lightmap baked with a sky light; the compiler does not bake one yet), a 'movable' one by the global distance field's. A write names the setting it changes, null its default; a value of another kind is refused by name.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { volumetricLightmap: false }) // the precomputed light off
// finest bricks streamed within 100 m of the view, 60 MB of them resident at most
world.volumetricLightmap = {
  volumetricLightmapLoadingRange: 100,
  volumetricLightmapBrickMemory: 60,
}
world.volumetricLightmap = { volumetricLightmap: null } // back to the default, on

Reference: world.volumetricLightmap.

global-distance-field.title: Global distance field
global-distance-field.description: The clipmaps composited from the meshes' distance fields around the camera, and the settings that size and update them.
global-distance-field.html:
world.globalDistanceField holds the settings of the global distance field, an option of createWorld too: the clipmaps composited from the meshes' distance fields around the camera (a mesh has one where its build sets distanceField) and the brick atlas those fields are streamed into. Lengths are in centimetres. Each setting is the reference's console variable of that name with its default: globalDistanceField (true), globalDistanceFieldUpdate (true), globalDistanceFieldClipmaps (4, at most 6), globalDistanceFieldViewDistance (20000), globalDistanceFieldClipmapExponent (2), globalDistanceFieldResolution (128), globalDistanceFieldMipFactor (4), globalDistanceFieldOccupancyRatio (0.3), globalDistanceFieldCacheMostlyStaticSeparately (true), globalDistanceFieldPartialUpdates (true), globalDistanceFieldStaggeredUpdates (true), globalDistanceFieldUpdatesPerFrame (2), globalDistanceFieldForceFullUpdate (false), globalDistanceFieldForceUpdateOnce (false), globalDistanceFieldFastCameraMode (false), globalDistanceFieldCameraVelocityDecay (0.7), globalDistanceFieldAverageCulledObjectsPerCell (512), globalDistanceFieldRecacheOnStreaming (true), globalDistanceFieldForceRecacheOnStreaming (false), globalDistanceFieldDebugShowStats (false), which writes over the upper right of the image the pages of the field — the most the atlas holds, those allocated and free, the pages of the clipmaps in use (combined), those among them with no surface and the pages composited this image (world.globalDistanceField = { globalDistanceFieldDebugShowStats: true }, null back to off), globalDistanceFieldStartDistance (100), globalDistanceFieldMinMeshRadius (20), globalDistanceFieldMinMeshRadiusInVoxels (0.5), the ones of the rays the reflections march through the field — globalDistanceFieldTraceResolution (252) and globalDistanceFieldTraceClipmapExtent (2500), the voxels along a clipmap and the first clipmap's half-extent while rays are marched, each next clipmap twice the one before, globalDistanceFieldTraceViewDistance (20000), the distance the scene is kept to then: the field makes one clipmap more than globalDistanceFieldClipmaps where the extent of the next reaches it, two more where the one after does (the default four clipmaps of 2500 become five at 40000 and six at 80000); while rays are marched, which the reflections do by default, globalDistanceFieldViewDistance, globalDistanceFieldClipmapExponent and globalDistanceFieldResolution have no effect, the three above size the clipmaps in their place, globalDistanceFieldCoveredExpandSurfaceScale (1) and globalDistanceFieldNotCoveredExpandSurfaceScale (0.6), the scale of the half voxel by which a ray expands the surface it meets in the pages the meshes cover and in those only two-sided meshes (foliage) reach, globalDistanceFieldSimpleCoverageBasedExpand (false), which reads the coverage atlas, the coverage of each voxel of such a page, and where true counts the whole page as not covered and leaves the atlas unread, globalDistanceFieldNotCoveredMinStepScale (4), the scale of its least step there, globalDistanceFieldDitheredTransparencyStepThreshold (0.5) and globalDistanceFieldDitheredTransparencyTraceThreshold (0.9), the noise under which a dithered ray is stopped there — and the atlas's meshDistanceFieldMaxObjectRadius (100000), meshDistanceFieldSurfaceBiasExpand (0.25), meshDistanceFieldBrickAtlasSize (128, a power of two, read when the atlas is made), meshDistanceFieldBrickAtlasDepth (32), meshDistanceFieldUploadKiB (8192), meshDistanceFieldBlockBricks (16, read when the atlas is made), meshDistanceFieldForceMips (0: follow the view; 1 to 3 loads that many mips of every mesh), meshDistanceFieldReverseAllocation (false) and runtimeMeshDistanceFields (false): a mesh made at run time, which no compiler gave a field, gets one built when it appears, on the page's GPU, by the compiler's own program (the same text, the same steps: the nearest triangle within the band, the 98 rays across the sphere for the sign; the voxels the device is in doubt of are measured again on the CPU, so the field is the compiler's). It is read when the scene's page records are made (a mesh cut at run time is flagged as having a field then) and each image after; set it with the world's other options before the scene opens. It costs the build once for each distinct mesh, in chunks short enough for the page's frames to go on, and the rays marched through the field meet the mesh a few frames after it appears. A mesh that deforms, one with no ray-tracing tree and one too deep for the program to walk get none. The reference builds fields at import only, so the setting is off until a scene asks for it. A write names the settings it changes, null one's default; a value of another kind is refused by name. A scene whose meshes built no distance field, and none asked for them at run time, is not touched.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { globalDistanceFieldClipmaps: 5 }) // one more clipmap
world.globalDistanceField = {
  globalDistanceFieldViewDistance: 40000,
  meshDistanceFieldUploadKiB: 16384,
}
world.globalDistanceField = { globalDistanceFieldFastCameraMode: true } // follow a fast camera, lower quality
world.globalDistanceField = { globalDistanceFieldFastCameraMode: null } // back to the default, off
// A cheaper march for the reflections: coarser clipmaps while rays are marched
world.globalDistanceField = { globalDistanceFieldTraceResolution: 140 }
// A scene kept to 800 m while rays are marched: the field grows from four clipmaps to six
world.globalDistanceField = { globalDistanceFieldTraceViewDistance: 80000 }
// Meshes made at run time (a generated terrain, a procedural prop) take part in the marched rays too
world.globalDistanceField = { runtimeMeshDistanceFields: true }
// Cheaper still, a page foliage reaches counted as not covered whole, the coverage atlas unread
world.globalDistanceField = { globalDistanceFieldSimpleCoverageBasedExpand: true }

Reference: world.globalDistanceField.

distance-field-occlusion.title: Distance field occlusion of the sky light
distance-field-occlusion.description: The sky light's occlusion found by cones traced against the distance fields: the settings of the trace.
distance-field-occlusion.html:
world.distanceFieldOcclusion holds the settings of the sky light's occlusion by the distance fields, an option of createWorld too: how much of the sky each pixel sees, from cones traced against the global field and the meshes' own fields, drawn when the sky light is movable and casts shadows, the bounce is off (with it on, its probes carry the sky and the screen probes its visibility) and a mesh built a distance field. The sky light then lights each pixel along the way its sky is most open and by the share of it the pixel sees: the sky's diffuse light is read along a normal turned toward that direction and scaled by the visibility, and the sky's reflection off a rough surface is occluded by the cone the sky leaves open (distanceFieldOcclusionSpecularMode: 0 by the share of sky seen, 1 by the intersection of the reflection's cone with the open one, skyLightSpecularOcclusionStrength its strength). The light's own settings shape it: occlusionMaxDistance, contrast, occlusionExponent, minOcclusion, occlusionTint and occlusionCombineMode. The settings below, each with its default; lengths are in centimetres: distanceFieldOcclusion (true), distanceFieldOcclusionQuality (2: 0 off, 1 the global field alone, 2 the meshes' fields too), distanceFieldOcclusionObjects (true), distanceFieldOcclusionStepExponentScale (0.5), distanceFieldOcclusionMaxViewDistance (20000, held to 65000), distanceFieldOcclusionViewFadeDistanceScale (0.7), distanceFieldOcclusionSampleSet (1), distanceFieldOcclusionJitterConeDirections (false), distanceFieldOcclusionUseJitter (true), distanceFieldOcclusionTraverseMips (true), distanceFieldOcclusionUseHistory (true), distanceFieldOcclusionHistoryStabilityPass (true), distanceFieldOcclusionHistoryWeight (0.85), distanceFieldOcclusionHistoryDistanceThreshold (30), distanceFieldOcclusionSpecularMode (1), skyLightSpecularOcclusionStrength (1, at least 0.1 where it is used) and distanceFieldOcclusionObjectsPerCullTile (512). A write names the settings it changes, null one's default; a value of another kind is refused by name. A scene whose meshes built no distance field is not touched.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { distanceFieldOcclusionQuality: 1 }) // the global field alone
world.distanceFieldOcclusion = { distanceFieldOcclusionMaxViewDistance: 40000 } // light pixels up to 400 m
world.distanceFieldOcclusion = { distanceFieldOcclusionUseHistory: false } // no temporal filter
world.distanceFieldOcclusion = { distanceFieldOcclusionQuality: null } // back to the default, 2

Reference: world.distanceFieldOcclusion.

surface-cache.title: Surface cache
surface-cache.description: The atlas that keeps the captured surface of the meshes' cards for the rays to read: its settings and what each costs.
surface-cache.html:
world.surfaceCache holds the settings of the surface cache, an option of createWorld too: the atlas that keeps the captured surface of the meshes' cards (flat boxes along a mesh's faces, built by the compiler), which the rays that leave the screen will read where they hit a mesh. Each setting is the reference's of that meaning, with its default, the row of the screen probes' level ultra (the default; cinematic holds the same); the level high holds another row of the atlas's side, the cards' density and resolutions, the lights a tile, the lighting's update factors and the radiosity's probes (SURFACE_CACHE_LEVEL_ROWS), which a setting you name overrides; lengths are in centimetres. The atlas: surfaceCacheAtlasSize (4096, texels a side, cut into pages of 128) and surfaceCacheResolution (1, from 0.5: a factor on the pages along a side, held between 1 and 64, and on the cards' resolutions). Which resolution a card is kept at, from its larger half side over the eye's distance, a metre at least: surfaceCacheCardTexelDensityScale (100), surfaceCacheCardMaxTexelDensity (0.2), surfaceCacheCardMaxResolution (512, up to 2048), surfaceCacheCardMinResolution (2), surfaceCacheOrthographicCardMinResolution (1: an orthographic view's own least, 0 takes the plain one), surfaceCacheSceneDetail (1, from 0.125 to 8: it divides the least resolution) and surfaceCacheCardCaptureMargin (0, added to the distance of the global distance field's outermost clipmap, past which a card is not kept). Which meshes get cards: surfaceCacheMeshCardsMinSize (10: the area a mesh's largest face must exceed is its square, a fifth of that for an emissive mesh) and surfaceCacheMeshCardsCullFaces (true: a card whose face is under that area is left out). A mesh a world cut at run time, which no compiler gave cards, has six axis-aligned cards made from its bounds, thickened by 5 cm, while runtimeMeshCards (true) is on; off, only the screen sees it in a reflection that leaves the screen. What an image does: surfaceCacheCardCapturesPerFrame (300 cards captured, the nearest first; the cards of twice as many meshes are added; 0 stops every capture), surfaceCacheRemovesPerFrame (512), surfaceCacheCardCaptureFactor (64: the atlas's texels over those of the atlas the captured pages are drawn in), surfaceCacheCardCaptureRefreshFraction (0.125: the share spent capturing pages again, the oldest first, to follow the materials), surfaceCacheCardCaptureEnableInvalidation (true), surfaceCacheNumFramesToKeepUnusedPages (256), surfaceCacheCompress (1: 1 and 2 keep the atlas's albedo, normal and emission in block-compressed textures, BC7, BC5 and BC6H, a quarter of those layers' memory, where the device has texture-compression-bc and leave it uncompressed elsewhere; 1 is compression by writing through a view of another format, which WebGPU cannot do, so it takes the block copy of 2, with the same result; 0 never), surfaceCacheAllowCardSharing (true: cards of one mesh with the same materials, face and proportions copy one capture), surfaceCacheAllowCardDownsampleFromSelf (true), surfaceCacheCaptureLodScaleFactor (1: the view's pixel error over it is the error the pages are drawn at), surfaceCacheResampleLighting (true), surfaceCacheDilationMode (0: 1 the two-sided meshes, 2 all), surfaceCacheDiffuseColorBoost (1, up to 4: the luminance of the albedo a read returns, raised to the power of its inverse) and surfaceCacheFastCameraMode (false: lower density, half the greatest resolution, twice the captures). The feedback that asks for finer pages: surfaceCacheFeedback (true), surfaceCacheFeedbackTileSize (16, raised to a power of two), surfaceCacheFeedbackMinPageHits (16), surfaceCacheFeedbackUniqueElements (1024) and surfaceCacheFeedbackResLevelBias (-0.5: levels added to the one a ray's cone calls for). The lighting of the cards' texels: surfaceCacheDirectLightingUpdateFactor (32) and surfaceCacheRadiosityUpdateFactor (64: the atlas's texels over the texels lit directly, and given indirect light, in an image, the pages left longest unlit first), surfaceCacheLightingUpdateSpeed (1, from 0.5 to 16: it divides both), surfaceCacheLightingQuality (1, from 0.5 to 6: it multiplies the radiosity probes' hemisphere by its square root and, from 6, halves their spacing), surfaceCacheLightingForceFullUpdate (false), surfaceCacheFreezeUpdateFrame (0; any other number stops the update clock and the pages' record of being lit, so that every image lights the same subset, for debugging), surfaceCacheLightingMaxDistanceFromFrustumToPrioritize (500, -1 never: the pages near the frustum are lit twice as soon), surfaceCacheLightingFeedback (true: a page the rays read at its finest level in the last two images is lit at the greatest update speed, 4, where the scene has acceleration structures and surfaceCacheDirectLightingHardwareRayTracing is on), surfaceCacheDirectLighting (true), surfaceCacheDirectLightingMaxLightsPerTile (8, up to 32, a power of two), surfaceCacheDirectLightingBatchShadows (2, from 0 to 2: the tiles of each light are gathered into a run before the masks and the light functions are made over them; at 2 the point lights', the spots' and the rectangles' tiles are each gathered by their type, at 0 and 1 each light has a run of its own; the image is the same), surfaceCacheDirectLightingGlobalSdfShadowRayBias (1: voxels the shadow ray starts off the surface, three where it grazes the light) and surfaceCacheDirectLightingCloudTransmittance (true).
