  heightFalloff: 300,
  albedo: [0.9, 0.95, 1],
  emissive: [0.02, 0.03, 0.05],
  startDistance: 20,
  sortPriority: 1,
})
session.setLocalFogVolume('valley', { radialDensity: 0.9 }) // the fields named replace the volume's own
session.localFogVolumes() // detached copies, in the order they were added
session.removeLocalFogVolume('valley')
FieldDefaultMeaning
id—Its name, unique among the local fog volumes.
matrixidentitySixteen numbers, column-major, its own space to the world's, metres. The sphere's radius is 5 m times the largest of the columns' lengths; its second column is the up the height law is measured along (the world's up is +y); shear and reflection are left out.
radialDensity1The extinction of the radial fog at the sphere's centre, per metre, ≥ 0 (held to it).
heightDensity1The extinction of the height fog at the sphere's height 0, per metre, ≥ 0 (held to it).
heightFalloff1000How fast the height fog thins out, ≥ 1 (held to it): the density is heightDensity · e^(−falloff / 100 · h), h the height in the sphere's radii.
heightOffset0The height, in radii, the height fog's density is heightDensity at.
scatteringDistribution0.2The phase function's g, in [0, 0.999] (held to it): 0 scatters equally every way, nearer 1 toward where the light goes.
albedowhiteThe share of the light each channel scatters, in [0, 1] (held to it).
emissiveblackThe light the medium gives off, a luminance, ≥ 0 per channel (held to it); it follows the medium's coverage.
startDistance0Metres from the eye before which the volume does not show, ≥ 0 (held to it); the run's localFogVolumeStartDistance holds it above that.
sortPriority0A whole number in [-127, 127] (held to it): a volume of a lower priority is drawn behind one of a higher, whatever their distance; equal priorities go farthest first.

The numbers are the reference's, in this engine's units: the reference writes distances in centimetres and densities per centimetre, here a start distance, the radius (5 m times the scale), the density cap and every extinction are metres and per metre, and the height axis is the matrix's second column in a world whose up is +y. A name already held is refused (DUPLICATE_SCENE_LOCAL_FOG_VOLUME), an unknown one (UNKNOWN_SCENE_LOCAL_FOG_VOLUME), a field that is null or not a finite number, a colour of three or a matrix of sixteen whose columns have a length (INVALID_SCENE_LOCAL_FOG_VOLUME). Like the lights and the objects of the volume, local fog volumes are declared at run time and are not part of a saved world; they can be declared whatever the settings below say, even with the project switch off, and then are never drawn.

Nine settings, those of the volumetric fog (world.volumetricFog…, setVolumetricFog), say how they are drawn; the first is the project's, read once when the session opens:

SettingDefaultMeaning
localFogVolumeSupporttrueThe project switch of the local fog volumes, read once when the session opens (changing it later changes nothing). Off, no program holds any of their code, not the sky light's capture's either, and no pass, buffer or block is made for them; they can still be declared, and are never drawn.
localFogVolumestrueWhether the local fog volumes are drawn.
localFogVolumeInVolumetrueWhether they are voxelised into the fog's volume where the scene's fog has one — the analytic law then draws only what lies past the volume's far end, and they lie under the volume's light. Off, the analytic law draws them whole, over the finished fog, the volume's light too.
localFogVolumeMaxVolumeDensity1The most extinction, per metre, a volume gives a cell of the fog's volume: its height law grows steepest at its bottom, and a dense cell makes the volume's history leak. 0 or more (held to it).
localFogVolumeStartDistance10Metres from the eye before which no local fog volume shows, whatever its own start distance; held to at least 0.1.
localFogVolumeMaxCount32The most volumes a view draws, the farthest and the lowest in priority dropped; held to 1…256.
localFogVolumeTileSize128The side, in pixels, of the tiles of the screen the volumes are culled by: each tile keeps the list of the volumes over it, and a pixel or a cell of the fog's volume walks its tile's list alone. Held to 8…512; the lists are made for the tile grid the view cuts, whatever its size.
localFogVolumeUsesDepthPyramidtrueWhether a tile's list drops a volume that lies wholly behind the surfaces the depth pyramid holds over it, so that no pixel walks a volume it cannot show. Off, or where the image has no pyramid, the tile's frustum alone culls.
localFogVolumeOnTranslucentfalseWhether translucent surfaces are fogged by them too; off, they are fogged by the scene's fog alone.
 
world.localFogVolumes = false // draw none of them, whatever the scene declares
world.localFogVolumeInVolume = false // keep them out of the fog's volume: drawn whole, over its light
world.localFogVolumeMaxVolumeDensity = 0.5 // no cell of the fog's volume takes more than 0.5 per metre of them
world.localFogVolumeStartDistance = 5 // the volumes show from five metres
world.localFogVolumeMaxCount = 64 // a view draws up to 64, the nearest and the highest in priority
world.localFogVolumeOnTranslucent = true // glass in the valley's fog is fogged by it too
world.localFogVolumeTileSize = 64 // smaller tiles: shorter lists, more tiles to cull (never fewer than 8 pixels)
world.localFogVolumeUsesDepthPyramid = false // cull by the tile's frustum alone
// The project switch is the session's, read once when it opens: off, no program holds any of the
// local fog volumes' code. A session that draws none of them is made so.
const world = createWorld('viewer', { localFogVolumeSupport: false }) // the project switch, at the session's opening

The tiles and their lists are the engine's: the view is cut into square tiles, and before the fog is laid one pass writes, for each, the volumes that can show over it (the sphere not wholly outside the tile's frustum, and, with localFogVolumeUsesDepthPyramid, not wholly behind the surfaces of the depth pyramid over its footprint). The image is the same as without the lists; the cost is per volume over a pixel's tile, not per volume the view draws. The lists live in a buffer made for the tile grid, only while a view draws a volume, and it counts in the bytes of that view's targets (metrics.views). The culling runs with the frame's other passes — it has no queue of its own to set — and no view of each tile's count of volumes is offered. The tile side asked for is never changed. Three diagnostics tell what the engine could not do, none of them stops the volumes being drawn:

DiagnosticMeaning and what to do
fog-local-tiles-too-largeThe lists for the tile grid would not fit a storage buffer of the device, so the view is not tiled and every pixel walks every volume of the view. Raise localFogVolumeTileSize; said once for a size.
fog-local-cull-failedThe culling pass did not compile: the same, untiled, until it does.
fog-local-sky-failedThe pass that gives the volumes the sky light's term did not compile: the term stays black, the sun and the volume's own light are drawn.

atmosphere-part.title: Atmosphere part
atmosphere-part.description: The planet's atmosphere: the sky, the haze of the distance and the tint of the sun's light, with every option.
atmosphere-part.html:
The atmosphere part fills the sky, hazes the distance and tints the sun's light through the air of a planet whose ground is the scene's plane y = 0. true is an Earth-like atmosphere, an object sets any field over those defaults — planet radius and air thickness in kilometres, scattering and absorption coefficients per kilometre, the ground's height in scene metres (groundHeight) and where its top stands on that plane (groundPosition, [x, z] in metres, [0, 0] by default):

world.scene.sky = { atmosphere: true } // the whole level: a part not named stays on
world.scene.sky = { sun: false, skyLight: false, heightFog: false, clouds: false } // the air alone
world.scene.sky = {
  atmosphere: { planetRadius: 6360, height: 60, mieAnisotropy: 0.8, groundHeight: 0 },
}
// A city 50 km from the world's origin: the planet's top under it, so the horizon curves from there
world.scene.sky = {
  atmosphere: { groundHeight: 120, groundPosition: [50_000, -12_000] },
}
world.scene.sky = { sun: { intensity: 10 }, heightFog: false, clouds: false } // the air, a sun, the sky's light
world.scene.sky = { atmosphere: false } // every part but the air
world.scene.sky = { atmosphere: { inMainView: false } } // the air lights the world but is not drawn in the view
world.scene.sky = { atmosphere: { holdout: true } } // with the alpha holdout on: the sky and its haze draw black and are a hole in the alpha

inMainView (on) says whether the sky, the sun's disk and the haze on the surfaces and the clouds are drawn in the view the camera sees. Off, none is: the sky is black, the fog alone over it, and nothing is hazed, while the sun's light tinted by the air and what the sky light captures of the air are as they are. holdout (off) makes the air hold its light out where the alpha holdout is in effect (the film settings primitiveAlphaHoldout and propagateAlpha): the sky draws black with the coverage of its air, which is laid on the image's alpha as a hole, and the haze on the surfaces and the clouds adds no light, dimming what lies behind it all the same.

The sun is the brightest directional light of index 0 (the second light is below), its colour times its intensity weighed by the eye's sensitivity to each channel, held as lights are added and removed (with an atmosphere or none): a light added replaces it only if brighter, and the sun removed gives its place to the brightest of the others, the first added of equals; atmosphereSun: false leaves one out. Where it is on, background is not shown, and the skyLight part lights the scene from the sky (without an atmosphere, from the background colour; below the horizon the sky itself, unless lowerHemisphereIsSolidColor is true (off by default, as in a new level's sky light): then lowerHemisphereColor, black, replaces it, lowerHemisphereCoverage, 1 by default, from 0 to 1, being the colour's alpha: how much of the colour replaces the sky and the clouds below the horizon, the rest of them showing through). The bounce is on by default (world.bounce, false turns it off): the sky light then reaches a surface only where the scene lets it — the street lit from above, the arcade dark — and a reflection that leaves the scene shows the sky; with the bounce off, the sky light lights every surface with the sky nothing hides.

The sky light can also light the scene with the scene itself: with realTimeCapture off and sourceType: 'capturedScene' it draws the scene once from its position into its cube, the six faces of a cube seen from there, the distance skyDistanceThreshold (150000 cm, the reference's default) the nearest it shows, and captureEmissiveOnly keeping only what the surfaces emit. It is captured when the light is created, when its cubemap or its angle changes and when realTimeCapture is switched; not when its colour, its intensity or its lower hemisphere changes, nor when it moves. A host that changed the world asks for the sky again by writing the part again:

world.scene.sky = {
  skyLight: { realTimeCapture: false, sourceType: 'capturedScene', cubemapResolution: 128 },
}

Its quality settings: skyLightCaptureSupersample (1, from 1 to 8) draws the faces larger and averages them down, skyLightCaptureLodDistanceScale (1) asks more detail of the scene in the faces. The faces trace no reflection of the scene. The model: sky light, captured scene.

world.scene.sky = {
  skyLight: {
    lowerHemisphereIsSolidColor: true,
    lowerHemisphereColor: [0.05, 0.04, 0.03],
    lowerHemisphereCoverage: 0.6,
  }, // a ground that lets 40% of the sky's light through
}

A sky light whose source is a specified cubemap (realTimeCapture: false, sourceType: 'specifiedCubemap') lights the scene with a picture the part holds as data: cubemap, { size, texels } — size texels across one face, from 1 to 1024, and texels the six faces in the order +x, −x, +y, −y, +z, −z of a cube texture looked up by the scene's own direction (+y up), each row by row from its top-left corner, three linear numbers ≥ 0 a texel (6 · size² · 3 numbers; a typed array or an array). The data is not copied: it must not be written after it is set. A host that moves between two pictures (two times of the day) adds cubemapBlend, { destination: { size, texels }, fraction }: the light reads the source mixed with the destination by fraction, 0 the source alone, 1 the destination alone, a value beyond held to them; write the part again to move the fraction. Saved worlds keep both (a typed array is saved as an array of its numbers). A malformed field is refused with TypeError naming it (skyLight: cubemap.texels expects 72 numbers, six faces of 2² texels).

const sky = new Float32Array(6 * 2 * 2 * 3).fill(0.4) // a 2×2 cube of one grey: the sky's radiance
world.scene.sky = {
  skyLight: {
    realTimeCapture: false,
    sourceType: 'specifiedCubemap',
    sourceCubemapAngle: 90, // degrees about the vertical
    cubemap: { size: 2, texels: sky },
  },
}
// later, toward the evening cube
world.scene.sky = {
  skyLight: {
    realTimeCapture: false,
    sourceType: 'specifiedCubemap',
    cubemap: { size: 2, texels: sky },
    cubemapBlend: { destination: { size: 2, texels: evening }, fraction: 0.25 },
  },
}

Nothing is clamped: where the brightest texel of a picture passes what a half float holds (65504), the engine writes the whole picture times the scale that brings that texel to 65504 and gives the light the inverse, so a sun texel of 1e6 lights the scene as 1e6, on any device; the two cubes of a blend share one scale, the brighter one's, so that the mix is of two lights in one unit. A cube of a large side is written face by face over several images from one buffer, and is the light's once its six faces are written. The part's data is the one source of the cube: the engine has no second entry for a texture the host makes.

The air holds two lights, a sun and a second one: a moon, or a second sun. Every directional light has an atmosphereSunIndex, 0 by default (1 for the second light); of the lights that may light the air (atmosphereSun not false) the brightest of each index is held, as the sun is: a light added takes the place of its index only if brighter, the light removed gives it to the brightest of the others of its index, the first added of equals, and a light moved to the other index is removed and added again. The sky, the haze over the distance, the sun disks and the sky light all take both lights. Index 1 held with none of index 0 is not moved to index 0: the second light shines alone. Any index other than 0 or 1 is refused (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT). SceneLight.atmosphereSunIndex carries the same value in a declared light (directional lights only).

world.scene.sky = { atmosphere: true, sun: false } // the scene's own lights are the air's
world.scene.add(light.directional({ intensity: 10, position: [-50, 70, 0] })) // the sun, index 0
const moon = light.directional({ intensity: 0.3, position: [60, 40, 20], atmosphereSunIndex: 1 })
world.scene.add(moon) // the second light of the air: its own sky, haze, disk and tint on what it lights
moon.atmosphereSunIndex = 0 // a write reaches the world at once; 0 is the default

A light's colour can follow a temperature: with useTemperature on, its colour is multiplied by that of a black body at temperatureKelvin (6500 by default, white; read between 1000 and 15000), and the sun, the sky and the fog take that colour. Three options say more of how a directional light meets the air: sunDiskTint (white, a linear colour) multiplies the sun's disk in the sky and never the light it gives; shadowsAir (off) lets the light's shadow shade the air — the haze and the sky's march read its shadow map along their rays, so that a mountain's shadow reaches into the haze, as atmosphereSampleLightShadowMap (on) allows; transmittancePerPixel (off) reads the air's transmittance toward the light for each surface point and not once at the ground, so that a low sun reddens a valley and not the summit above it. A saved world keeps each of them.

A light draws light shafts through nine fields, each written to its record and to a saved world only when it differs from its default. shaftOcclusion (off) lets the light darken the fog's inscattering where the scene hides it: shaftOcclusionDarkness (0.05) is what a full occlusion maps to, 1 darkening nothing, and everything nearer the eye than shaftOcclusionDepthRange (1000 metres) occludes; shaftOverrideDirection ([0, 0, 0], a vector) names, when it is not zero, the direction the shafts come from instead of the light's own. These four belong to a directional light alone. shaftBloom (off) adds a bloom around any light: shaftBloomScale (0.2) is the factor on the colour it adds, shaftBloomThreshold (0) the brightness the image must pass after exposure to bloom, shaftBloomMaxBrightness (100) the brightness above which it is brought down, and shaftBloomTint (white, a linear colour) the factor on its colour. A vector is changed in place with set, as sunDiskTint is.

const sun = light.directional({ intensity: 10, position: [-50, 70, 0], castShadow: true })
sun.shaftOcclusion = true
sun.shaftOcclusionDepthRange = 2000 // metres
sun.shaftOverrideDirection.set(-0.3, 0.4, 0.1) // the shafts come from there
sun.shaftBloom = true
sun.shaftBloomTint.set([1, 0.85, 0.6])
world.addLight({ id: 'lamp', kind: 'point', intensity: 50, position: [0, 3, 0], shaftBloom: true })
const sun = light.directional({ intensity: 10, position: [-50, 70, 0], castShadow: true })
sun.useTemperature = true
sun.temperatureKelvin = 5200 // a warmer white
sun.sunDiskTint.set([1, 0.8, 0.6]) // the disk redder than the light it gives
sun.shadowsAir = true // the mountains' shadows in the haze
world.addLight({
  id: 'moon',
  kind: 'directional',
  direction: [0.2, -1, 0.1],
  color: [0.7, 0.8, 1],
  intensity: 0.3,
  atmosphereSunIndex: 1,
  temperatureKelvin: 4100,
  useTemperature: true,
})

The air's samples are scaled by sampleCountScale (1, from 0.25): the caps its quality settings give the marches (below) are no more than 32 times it, and the haze volume's samples a slice no more than twice it. The air's quality is the sky's quality settings of world.skyQuality — atmosphereOn (on), the samples of a march through the air (atmosphereSamplesMin, atmosphereSamplesMax, atmosphereDistanceToMaxSamplesKm), of the sky table (skyTableSamplesMin, skyTableSamplesMax, skyTableDistanceToMaxSamplesKm) and of a slice of the haze volume (aerialSamplesPerSlice), the sizes of the tables (transmittanceWidth, transmittanceHeight, multiScatterWidth, multiScatterHeight, skyTableWidth, skyTableHeight) and of the haze volume (aerialWidth, aerialDepthSlices, aerialDepthKm), the samples that build the transmittance and the multiple-scattering tables (transmittanceSamples, multiScatterSamples), and the switches skyTableFast (the sky read from its table, else every sky pixel marched), aerialFastOnOpaque (on; off, a pass over the lit image marches the haze of each opaque pixel from the eye to its depth, jittered by the blue noise and shaded by the shadow maps and the clouds, the translucent surfaces reading the volume either way), aerialDepthTest, transmittanceTable, transmittanceSmallFormat (the table in four 8-bit channels), distantSkyLightTable and distantSkyLightAltitudeKm (the fog's sky, made every image), multiScatterHighQuality (8 directions over the sphere), skyTablesFullPrecision (the haze volume in 32-bit floats) and atmosphereSampleLightShadowMap —, whose defaults are the reference's fourth level (max) and which the smooth, balanced and fine presets set to its lower three and the cinematic preset to its fifth:

world.quality.preset = 'fine' // the effects' level 2: 2 samples a slice, 64 samples at most
world.skyQuality = { skyTableFast: false, atmosphereSamplesMax: 256 } // every sky pixel marched
world.scene.sky = { atmosphere: { sampleCountScale: 2 } } // twice the samples, within those caps
world.skyQuality = { skyTableFast: null } // given back to the preset

The cinematic preset is the fifth level of the effects group (smooth, balanced, fine and max are its levels 0 to 3): it marches every sky pixel and the haze on the opaque surfaces instead of reading their tables, and writes these values (SKY_PRESET_LEVELS.effects.cinematic):

world.quality.preset = 'cinematic' // the same values, written by the level
world.skyQuality = {
  aerialSamplesPerSlice: 8,
  aerialDepthSlices: 32,
  skyTableFast: false, // every sky pixel is marched
  aerialFastOnOpaque: false,
  skyTableSamplesMin: 4,
  skyTableSamplesMax: 256,
  atmosphereSamplesMin: 8,
  atmosphereSamplesMax: 256,
  transmittanceSmallFormat: false,
  transmittanceSamples: 30,
  multiScatterSamples: 20,
}

Ranges. planetRadius, height, rayleighScaleHeight and mieScaleHeight are above 0 (a height under 0.1 km is read as 0.1 km, the thinnest air), mieAnisotropy is between −1 and 1 (the bounds themselves are refused: at ±1 the phase function's denominator is 0 straight along the ray, so the open range is kept), aerialPerspectiveStartDepth is 0 or more, multiScatteringFactor is from 0 to 100 and minSunElevation from −90° to 90°. A value outside refuses with the range in its message; a world saved with an anisotropy of −0.3 or a radius of 12000 km loads and draws.

The planet's place. The planet is a sphere under the plane y = groundHeight, its top at groundPosition; a planet that is to have its centre at a place is given that place with a groundHeight its radius (in metres) over it. The three ways to place a planet (its top at the world's origin, its top at a place, its centre at a place) are this one setting.

The view from above the air. An eye above the air (higher than planetRadius + height) is not brought down into it: the air is seen from outside, the planet's limb with its blue edge, the sun's disk through the air at the limb, the haze and the clouds along a ray from where it enters the air; a ray that never enters it sees black. An eye under the ground is held five metres over it. Under an orthographic camera the sky, the haze and the clouds are drawn as well, each pixel's ray starting at the pixel's own point (the air under an orthographic camera).

A field out of range is refused (INVALID_SCENE_ENVIRONMENT); to change a field, write scene.sky again. SceneEnvironment.atmosphere carries the same fields. The model: atmosphere and sky light.

Reference: world.bounce, world.skyQuality.

clouds-part.title: Clouds part
clouds-part.description: One layer of clouds marched from the eye, seen in the view, in the shadows and in the sky light: every option.
clouds-part.html:
The clouds part is one layer of clouds ray marched from the eye: in the view, in its shadow maps and in the sky light's capture, whether or not the scene has an atmosphere. true is the level's layer; an object sets fields of the layer and of its material over the defaults of the parts table. It is drawn while the sky quality's cloudsOn is on (the default), read again at each image. The wind drifts the clouds by the world's time, the clock the material graphs read: a paused world holds them still. Under an orthographic camera the layer is traced directly, a ray for each pixel.

Clouds with no atmosphere. With none they stand on a planet of planetRadiusKm (6360 by default) under the plane y = 0: the sun and the second light's own illuminance reaches them (a transmittance of one), there is no haze on them and sunTintPerSample has no effect, and the distant sky light that lights them (cloudDistantSkyLight) is the sky light's own diffuse light, not read from an air. The lights of the air are packed for the clouds only while a clouds part is followed.

world.scene.sky = { atmosphere: false, clouds: true, sun: true } // clouds over a planet with no air

How the lights shade the cloud. rayMarchVolumeShadow (default true) says how the cloud is shaded by the air's lights, in the view and in the sky light's capture. On, a ray is marched through the material from each sample toward each light (shadowSamplesScale, shadowRayLengthKm): the exact shade, dearer. Off, no ray is marched: each sample reads the clouds' shadow map of the light (the sky quality's cloudShadowMap, the light's castCloudShadows and cloudShadowStrength), its optical depth d letting exp(-d) of the light through for the first order of scattering and exp(-d · e^n) for the order n, e being multiScatterOcclusion. A light with no map (the setting off, the light not casting cloud shadows) then shades nothing. The programs are made for the choice, so changing it compiles them again once. What the shadow map serves besides, in both settings: the air's march (the sky, the haze, the distant sky light), the surfaces' direct light, the fog's light and the translucent surfaces; with the switch on, the cloud's own shade is marched and the map is not read by the cloud.

// Cheaper clouds: read the shadow map instead of marching toward the sun.
world.modules.set('sky', { clouds: { rayMarchVolumeShadow: false } })
// The shadow map is then what shades the clouds, so keep it on and give the sun a map:
world.skyQuality = { cloudShadowMap: true }

The sky light on the underside. undersideSkyLoss (0.5, from 0 to 1) is how much of the distant sky light the underside of a cloud loses where the cloud's material gives no occlusion of its own. The built-in material always gives one (ambientOcclusion, 0.5), so no cloud of it reads the setting.

The sun's shadow in the opaque scene. skyLightShadowFromOpaque (off) acts on the clouds of the sky light's capture as well as on its sky: the clouds read the sun's shadow map where cloudSampleLightShadowMap is on and the first light of the air casts a shadow that is projected this image.

The sky meshes of the capture. skyLightDepthBuffer (on) gives the faces of the real-time capture a depth buffer where they show the scene's sky meshes (the surfaces of a sky material): the meshes cover each other by their distance, and the height fog is laid over each pixel at the distance of the mesh drawn there, an endless ray only where no mesh is. Off, the meshes are painted in their sort order and the fog is laid along an endless ray.

// Fog at the true distance of the sky dome in the sky light's capture (the default); off lays it along an endless ray.
world.skyQuality = { skyLightDepthBuffer: false }

The settings. cloudShadowMapSpatialFiltering (1, read from 0 to 4), cloudShadowMapNewFrameWeight (1, read from 0 to 1), cloudLocalLightShadowSamples (12, read from 0 to 128), cloudRenderTargetScale (1, read from 0.1 to 1) and cloudEmptySpaceSkippingDepthKm (40, read from 1) take any number and are read held to the range, as the console variables they come from are: 8 filter passes is 4, a weight of 2 is 1. The sky occlusion map's settings (cloudSkyAO, cloudSkyAOResolutionMax, cloudSkyAOTraceSamples, cloudSkyAOFiltering, cloudSkyAOSnapKm) are in the sky module. Removed, because nothing in the engine could read them: lightShaftAfterDof (the shafts are added to the lit image; the other image the switch could send them to, a translucency drawn apart, does not exist here), and the sky light's indirectLightingIntensity, samplesPerPixel, affectReflection and affectGlobalIllumination (the reference reads them in its ray-traced and path-traced lighting only). A scene or a call naming one is refused with the field's name.

The empty-space table. cloudEmptySpaceSkipping (off) builds, before each view's tracing, a table of where the clouds start (32 × 32 texels over the view, cloudEmptySpaceSkippingDepthKm deep in 64 slices), and the march of a ray begins there; never in a reflection. cloudEmptySpaceSkippingSliceBias (0) moves the start by that many slices, −1 one slice toward the eye, and cloudEmptySpaceSkippingCorners (on) reads the corners of each cell as well as its centre. The built-in material leaves the table's input unconnected, and an unconnected input says matter is everywhere, so its table holds only the first slice's start moved by the bias (0 by default): the image is the one without the table, for the cost of the pass.

world.skyQuality = { cloudEmptySpaceSkipping: true } // the table is built each image
world.skyQuality = { cloudEmptySpaceSkippingSliceBias: 2, cloudEmptySpaceSkippingCorners: false }
world.skyQuality = { cloudEmptySpaceSkipping: null } // given back to the preset

On the translucent surfaces. The clouds are composed over the lit image before the transparents are drawn, so a translucent surface behind a cloud would be drawn over it. Two things lay them right, both read per vertex:

  • cloudShadowOnTranslucent (a project switch, false by default, read once when the session opens): the clouds' shadow maps also shade the translucent surfaces. The shade of the forward directional light (below) is read from its clouds' shadow map at each vertex of a translucent surface and interpolated over the triangle, so it costs a vertex a map read and a pixel nothing. It applies where the forward light is one of the air's two lights that has a map this image: the sky quality's cloudShadowMap on (the default), the light's castCloudShadows on (off by default) and its cloudShadowOnSurfaceStrength above 0 (1 by default, the factor on how much of the shade the surfaces take). Like every run-time setting it is advertised to the tools by runtimeToolsSchema (field cloudShadowOnTranslucent, the "effects" quality group, no preset writes it) and held in the sky quality rules.
  • cloudFog (a material option, false by default): a see-through (transparent) surface that is fogged (fog not false) receives the clouds in front of it as part of its fog — the cloud image is laid over the fog of each vertex of the surface, faded in over cloudSoftBlendingDistanceOnTranslucent kilometres from the cloud's front, so a surface behind a cloud is seen through it, not over it. A rough approximation that helps where a translucent surface lies behind a cloud (a window seen through a cloud bank, a particle sprite beyond a cloud); the surface needs the vertices to carry it, so a very large triangle shows the cloud at its corners only. Setting it on a material of a scene changes its blended programs, like allowNegativeEmissive changes the graph's.

cloudFogLateOnTranslucent (off), with cloudFogLate on and a trace size that rebuilds the image ('quarterToHalf', 'quarterToFull'): the surfaces whose material has cloudFog read the cloud image with the fog already laid on it, which the rebuild writes as one more image of the rebuilt size; off, they read the image without the fog (the fog is laid on the clouds only when they are composed over the lit image), so a translucent surface behind a cloud can show with another fog than the cloud's. cloudSoftBlendingDistanceOnTranslucent (0.5), read from 0.0001, is the kilometres, from the cloud's front, over which the cloud fades in over a translucent surface behind it. Off, the programs that draw a translucent surface hold none of this code; with either on, they read both per vertex, the one that is off giving its neutral value.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { cloudShadowOnTranslucent: true }) // the shade: a project switch
// The sun has a cloud shadow map, and lets the surfaces take all of its shade:
world.scene.sky = { clouds: true, sun: { castCloudShadows: true, cloudShadowOnSurfaceStrength: 1 } }
// A glass pane in the scene now darkens under a cloud's shadow; at 0.5 it would take half of it:
world.scene.sky = {
  clouds: true,
  sun: { castCloudShadows: true, cloudShadowOnSurfaceStrength: 0.5 },
}

const glass = material.meshStandard({
  transparent: true,
  opacity: 0.4,
  cloudFog: true, // the clouds in front of the glass are laid over its fog
})
world.skyQuality = {
  cloudFogLateOnTranslucent: true, // the image the translucent surfaces read has the fog on it
  cloudSoftBlendingDistanceOnTranslucent: 1, // 1 km to fade a cloud in over a surface behind it
}
world.skyQuality = { cloudFogLateOnTranslucent: null } // given back to the preset

The model: the clouds in the air and the sky light and the transparent surfaces.

declared-lights.title: Declared lights
declared-lights.description: Add, change and remove lights like any object: the SceneLight fields, their units and their defaults.
declared-lights.html:
Lights are added, changed and removed like any object. Each is a SceneLight (version 4): point and spot carry position and range in metres, spot also direction, an outerConeAngle and an innerConeAngle, half-angles in radians; rect carries position, range, the direction of its face's normal, its width axis right and its size (width, height; a side under 1 cm lights and casts as one of 1 cm, the light keeping what you declared); directional only direction (of propagation), refused with a position, range or a cone angle. All carry linear color, an intensity and castsShadow, a rectangle too. A directional may also carry shadowDistance (A sun's shadow distance) atmosphereSunIndex (Atmosphere part) and forwardShadingPriority (below), refused on any other kind.

Intensity and its unit. A directional light's intensity is in lux, 10 when it names none. A point, a spot and a rect write theirs in intensityUnits (the node form's intensityUnits, refused on a directional), one of five, 'unitless' by default:

intensityUnitsWhat the number isThe light it gives
'candelas'A luminous intensity.The number, in candelas.
'lumens'A luminous flux.Spread over the solid angle it fills: a point's sphere (4π), a spot's cone (2π (1 − cos of its outer cone)), a rect's cosine lobe (π).
'nits'A luminance.Times the source's area: a point or spot's sphere or capsule, 4π r (r + length / 2) of its emitterRadius and emitterLength (none without a radius); a rect's face.
'ev'An exposure value at ISO 100, any finite number.2 to that power, in candelas (a luminance over an implicit square metre).
'unitless'The default scale.16 candelas for every 10 000.

A lamp that names no intensity is the light a new one is placed with, 5000 unitless, written in its unit: 8 candelas, 8 × 4π ≈ 100.5 lumens for a point (8 × π ≈ 25.1 for a rect), an EV of 3 (log2 8) and 8 candelas over the source's area in nits. A rect lights by the radiance of its candelas over half its face's area; the node form's rectangle is 64 cm a side by default. A point or a spot taken off the inverse square (inverseSquared: false) takes its intensity as it is, a brightness in no unit: there it is at least 0 in any unit, and a default in EV or nits is 8. Elsewhere the intensity is at least 0, but any number in EV. A point or spot in nits under the inverse square needs an emitterRadius: with no source it would give no light, and is refused (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT). The node form (light.point(…), light.spot(…), light.rectArea(…), light.directional(…)) has the same defaults; an ambient, hemisphere or probe light's intensity is 1. A version-2 rect's intensity was its radiance: a radiance L is L / 2 nits, which a saved scene of before version 4 is read as (one with no radiance is refused, UNSUPPORTED_SCENE_FORMAT). A lamp saved before version 5 that named no unit was in candelas, and is read as such.

light.point({ position: [0, 3, 0] }) // 5000 unitless, 8 candelas
light.spot({ intensity: 800, intensityUnits: 'lumens', position: [0, 3, 0] }) // 800 lumens through its cone
world.addLight({
  id: 'sun',
  kind: 'directional',
  color: [1, 1, 1],
  direction: [0, -1, 0],
  castsShadow: true,
}) // 10 lux

Two options of every light say how the volumetric fog and the clouds take it, over the light on surfaces, which they never change: fogScattering (default 1, 0 or more) is the factor on its colour in the fog volume and in the clouds' local lights, and a light of 0 is left out of both; shadowsFog (default true for a directional light, false for any other) lets a light that casts a shadow shadow the fog too. The sky light has the same factor, its part's volumetricScatteringIntensity (1 by default): the factor on the sky the fog scatters. A saved world keeps a shadowsFog set against its kind's default; fogScattering is among the light's numbers.

const lamp = light.point({ intensity: 20, position: [0, 3, 0], distance: 12, castShadow: true })
lamp.fogScattering = 0.5 // half of it in the fog and the clouds; 0 leaves it out of both
lamp.shadowsFog = true // its shadow map also shadows the fog volume (a sun's does by default)
world.scene.sky = { skyLight: { volumetricScatteringIntensity: 0 } } // the fog scatters none of the sky light

The same in the declared form: world.addLight({ id: 'lamp', kind: 'point', ..., fogScattering: 0.5, shadowsFog: true }); a negative fogScattering or a shadowsFog that is not a boolean is refused (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT). A rect takes shadowsFog as a point does, and refuses emitterRadius, emitterLength, emitterSoftRadius and emitterAxis (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT): they describe the source of a point or a spot, a rectangle's source is its size.

A directional light takes softAngle (degrees, from 0 up to, not including, 180; default 0), the soft angle of its disk: it widens the highlight the sun leaves on a glossy surface without lighting more of the surface, as emitterSoftRadius does for a point or a spot. A point, a spot or a rect refuses it (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT).

const sun = light.directional({ intensity: 6, softAngle: 2 }) // a broader highlight on polished surfaces

A point or a spot takes a light profile, the shape of the light a lamp gives as a photometric file measured it (an IES file the compiler turned into a profile, a lamp of an imported scene that names one has it already): iesProfile is the profile's id, useIesBrightness (default false) makes the light's intensity the profile's brightness (its greatest candela, iesBrightness: a finite number above 0 that the compiler writes with the profile, and only beside iesProfile) times iesBrightnessScale (default 1, from 0) in place of intensity, written in the light's unit; a light that carries no iesBrightness keeps its intensity. The colour of the light is multiplied, for each direction it leaves in, by the profile's share of its greatest candela there, so a profiled light lights nothing a profile says it does not. The profile is read in the light's own frame: its vertical axis is the direction of the light, its 0 degree vertical angle (the nadir) straight ahead along the way the light shines, and its horizontal angles run round that axis, laid out from emitterAxis, the light's own up, which is also the axis of its tube where it has an emitterLength. A light that names a profile therefore needs both a direction and an emitterAxis, and the axis may not be parallel to the direction (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT); a sun or a rect refuses the profile's fields. The profiles are held in one atlas (world.lightProfile, below) of at most lightProfileAtlasMaxProfiles (32) of them at once; a light whose profile is not among them, or not loaded yet, lights as a lamp with none. A scene with no profiled light compiles no profile code and binds no atlas. The translucent surfaces do not read the profile: they are lit as by a lamp with none.

world.addLight({
  id: 'downlight',
  kind: 'spot',
  position: [0, 3, 0],
  direction: [0, -1, 0],
  emitterAxis: [1, 0, 0], // the light's own up: the profile's horizontal angles are laid round the direction from it
  iesProfile: 'downlight.ies', // a profile the compiler wrote from the file
  useIesBrightness: true, // the intensity is the profile's greatest candela...
  iesBrightnessScale: 0.5, // ...times 0.5
})

world.lightProfile holds the settings of the profiles' atlas, each an option of createWorld too, with the reference's default: lightProfileAtlasResolution (256, from 16 to 4096: the texels a side of a slice; a profile of another side is resampled to it, bilinear, when it is written) and lightProfileAtlasMaxProfiles (32, from 1 to 32: the most profiles the atlas holds). The atlas is made with the slices the lights ask (one per distinct profile, up to that most) and no more, made again, with every profile written into it again, when more are asked than it was made with or a setting moves, and handed back when no light names a profile any more. An agent sets them through trillion3d_set_light_profile.

world.lightProfile = { lightProfileAtlasResolution: 128 } // lighter slices, a softer profile
world.lightProfile = { lightProfileAtlasMaxProfiles: 8 } // at most 8 profiles; a ninth lights as a lamp with none

Reference: SceneLight, world.lightProfile.

simple-lights.title: Simple lights
simple-lights.description: Lights the host hands to an image without adding them to the scene: a particle's, an effect's.
simple-lights.html:
A simple light is a light the host hands to an image and the scene does not hold: a particle's, an effect's. It is a point light with no shadow, no light function, no profile and no source size, in every lighting channel. It lights the opaque surfaces and the see-through ones, the volumetric fog (by volumetricScatteringIntensity) and, where affectsTranslucency is on, the translucency lighting volume; it feeds no shadow map, no indirect bounce and no ray traced pass, and the list changes at every image without staling any cache of the scene's lights. A scene that holds only simple lights is lit, not shown unlit.

world.setSimpleLights(entries) replaces the list; it lasts until another is given. Each entry: position and radius in metres, color (linear RGB times the strength; under the inverse square a colour of 1 is 1e-4 candela, the scale the reference writes particle lights in with distances in centimetres), exponent (0, the inverse square windowed by the radius; above 0, one less the squared distance over the squared radius to that power), inverseExposureBlend (0, from 0 to 1), volumetricScatteringIntensity (0), specularScale and diffuseScale (1, not bounded above) and affectsTranslucency (false: the light is injected into the translucency lighting volume, on the classic and the sampled paths alike), allowSampledLighting (false: see sampledSimpleLights below), sampledCastsShadow (false: where the sampled lighting takes the light, it traces a shadow ray for it against the scene's geometry; the light holds no shadow map) and lightId ({ localId, sourcePrimitiveId }, two whole numbers of at least 0, absent by default: the identity the sampled lighting follows the light by from one image to the next, through the changes of order and of count of the list, to read the history of the same light; a light with none has no history; two lights of a list may not share one, each view follows the lights by it on its own). An entry whose radius and colour are both nothing is left out. A list equal to the one held changes nothing: the images held stay. A list that changes at every image draws the next image again and nothing else: no cache of the scene's lights, no shadow map and no capture of the reflections is invalidated by it, and only the simple lights' slots go to the GPU.

world.simpleLight holds the settings, each an option of createWorld too, with the reference's default: allowSimpleLights (true: the lights are taken; off, an image lights nothing by them), hairSimpleLights (true: the hair strands are lit by them) and sampledSimpleLights (1: where a view lights with the sampled lighting, 0 leaves every simple light to the classic pass, 1 hands it the ones whose entry sets allowSampledLighting, so none unless an entry does, 2 hands it all; a simple light the sampled lighting does not take is lit by the classic local lights' pass).

world.setSimpleLights(
  sparks.map((p, i) => ({
    position: p.position,
    radius: 2,
    color: [4, 2, 0.5],
    exponent: 0,
    affectsTranslucency: true,
    allowSampledLighting: true, // the sampled lighting takes it (with the default sampledSimpleLights 1)
    sampledCastsShadow: true, // and traces a shadow ray for it
    lightId: { localId: i, sourcePrimitiveId: emitter }, // its history follows it as the list reorders
  })),
)
world.simpleLight = { hairSimpleLights: false } // the strands ignore them
world.simpleLight = { allowSimpleLights: false } // none are lit
world.simpleLight = { sampledSimpleLights: 2 } // the sampled lighting takes every simple light

Reference: world.simpleLight.

rectangle-light-pictures.title: Rectangle lights' pictures
rectangle-light-pictures.description: Map a picture on a rectangle light's face, for a window, a screen or a gobo: the fields and what each does.
rectangle-light-pictures.html:
A rect light may name a picture mapped on its face, which its colour is multiplied by wherever it lights (a window, a screen, a gobo): sourceTexture (the id the picture was registered under), sourceTextureScale ([1, 1], each from above 0 to 1: the share of the picture shown) and sourceTextureOffset ([0, 0], each from 0 to 1: where the share starts). Seen from the front of the light, the picture runs left to right along right and its top edge lies toward cross(direction, right). Any other kind refuses the three fields; a scale or an offset without a sourceTexture is refused (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT). The host registers the picture, an ImageBitmap or any image the engine can copy to a texture, with world.setRectLightTexture(id, image) (null forgets it; a light whose picture is not registered lights as a plain rectangle) and says it changed in place with world.refreshRectLightTexture(id). The pictures of all the lights are kept in one square atlas, a slot each (a picture named by several lights, with the same share, is one slot), packed without overlap with the holes of the freed slots reused first, with a chain of mip levels the lighting reads by the solid angle the rectangle covers. The diffuse light, the specular lobe (also under a clear coat, a cloth's fuzz or a subsurface profile), the thin surfaces' transmission, the cards of the surface cache and the sampled lighting read the picture; the volumetric fog tints the light of the rectangle by it while volumetricFogRectLightTexture (false by default, a setting of the volumetric fog, world.volumetricFog…) is on: each cell reads the picture along the mean direction of the rectangle's light (the direction of its form factor with no normal), at the level the solid angle it covers asks; the translucent surfaces' forward programs (the blends) read it where the device grants 17 sampled textures a shader stage, which the session asks of an adapter that offers them; on an adapter that stops at 16 they light the rectangle plain (declared fallback: the widest blend program, with display layers, already binds the sixteen guaranteed); the translucency lighting volume lights the rectangle plain, and the reflections' and the bounce's rays take the light of the surface cache, which holds the picture.

world.rectLightAtlas holds the settings of the atlas, each an option of createWorld too, with the reference's default: rectLightAtlasMaxResolution (4096, from 64 to 16384: the most texels a side; past it the pictures are packed a mip level smaller until they fit), rectLightAtlasFilterQuality (0 a box of 2 by 2 texels, 1 a Gaussian approximation), rectLightAtlasMaxTextureRatio (2, from 1 to 16: the most a picture may be wider than high, or higher than wide, before its short side is stretched), rectLightAtlasFormat (0 11, 11 and 10 bits, faster, the hue may shift, kept as 16-bit floats on a device that cannot draw into it; 1 four 16-bit floats), sampledLightsTexturedRectLights (true), and the switches rectLightAtlasForceUpdate, rectLightAtlasResetOnChange, rectLightAtlasClear, rectLightAtlasDebugClear (magenta in a new atlas), rectLightAtlasDebug and rectLightAtlasDebugMipLevel (the debug view, below), all off or 0.

world.setRectLightTexture('window', await createImageBitmap(blob))
world.addLight({
  id: 'window-light',
  kind: 'rect',
  position: [0, 2.5, 0],
  direction: [0, -1, 0],
  right: [1, 0, 0],
  size: [2, 1],
  range: 12,
  intensity: 8,
  sourceTexture: 'window', // the picture registered above
  sourceTextureScale: [0.5, 1], // the left half of it
  sourceTextureOffset: [0, 0],
})
world.rectLightAtlas = { rectLightAtlasMaxResolution: 2048, rectLightAtlasFilterQuality: 1 }
world.rectLightAtlas = { rectLightAtlasDebug: true } // draws the atlas over the image
world.volumetricFogRectLightTexture = true // the fog's cells tint a rectangle's light by its picture

transmission (default false) makes a light shine through the subsurface-profile surfaces it shadows (their transmission: the light that crosses the thickness behind the lit side, ears, fingers, wax). It acts on a light that is movable and casts a shadow, and on no other: a stationary or static light has its shadow baked or held still, without the thickness the transmission needs. A saved world keeps a transmission that is on.

const lamp = light.point({
  intensity: 20,
  position: [0, 3, 0],
  distance: 12,
  castShadow: true,
  mobility: 'movable',
})
lamp.transmission = true // the profile surfaces it shadows glow where its light goes through them

The same in the declared form: world.addLight({ id: 'lamp', kind: 'point', ..., mobility: 'movable', castsShadow: true, transmission: true }); a transmission that is not a boolean is refused (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT).

Every light has a mobility: 'static' (meant to be baked into the lightmaps: it neither moves nor changes and casts no dynamic shadow), 'stationary' (it does not move, its colour and intensity may change; the default of every light kind) or 'movable' (fully dynamic). Any other value is refused (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT); a saved world keeps a mobility other than the default. The volumetric lightmap reads it to know which directional light's shadowing it holds (mobilityOf(light), scene/light/fields.ts).

const lamp = light.point({ intensity: 20, position: [0, 3, 0], distance: 12 })
lamp.mobility = 'movable' // 'static' | 'stationary' (the default) | 'movable'
world.addLight({
  id: 'lamp2',
  kind: 'point',
  color: [1, 1, 1],
  intensity: 20,
  castsShadow: false,
  position: [0, 3, 0],
  range: 12,
  mobility: 'static',
})

A rectangle light casts a shadow like a point light: one cube of six faces centred on it, as far as its range. A surface behind the rectangle's plane is outside its shadow region (a surface exactly in the plane is in front: the rectangle lights it), and a surface turned away from it is not shadowed by it. Its penumbra is traced toward its centre through a cone whose radius is half its width; shadowRayCountLocal and shadowSamplesPerRayLocal set its rays and steps, as for any local light. The two forms of a light below are the same panel, 2 m by 1 m, three metres up, facing down, its shadow as deep as 12 metres (the node form's distance is the range of the declared one):

const panel = light.rectArea({
  width: 2,
  height: 1,
  intensity: 30,
  position: [0, 3, 0],
  distance: 12,
  castShadow: true,
})
panel.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2 // a node's face looks down its −z: turned to look down −y
panel.shadowsFog = true // its shadow map also shadows the fog volume
world.addLight({
  id: 'panel',
  kind: 'rect',
  position: [0, 3, 0],
  range: 12,
  direction: [0, -1, 0],
  right: [1, 0, 0],
  size: [2, 1],
  color: [1, 1, 1],
  intensity: 30,
  castsShadow: true,
  shadowsFog: true,
})

shadowResolutionScale (1, a number of 0 or more; a point, a spot or a rect; refused on a sun) is the factor on the resolution the light's shadow is given. It decides whether the light takes a shadow and how it fades with its size on the screen (see Local lights' shadow gates): 0 takes the shadow away, a number above 1 keeps a far light's shadow longer, one below 1 lets it go sooner. A saved scene keeps it when it is not 1.

const lamp = light.point({ intensity: 20, position: [0, 3, 0], distance: 12, castShadow: true })
lamp.shadowResolutionScale = 2 // keeps its shadow farther than a lamp left at 1
world.addLight({
  id: 'far',
  kind: 'point',
  position: [0, 3, 90],
  range: 12,
  color: [1, 1, 1],
  intensity: 20,
  castsShadow: true,
  shadowResolutionScale: 0.5,
})

Of the directional lights of a scene, one is the forward light: the one the volumetric fog is lit by and the one the clouds' shade on translucent surfaces follows. It is the light of the highest forwardShadingPriority (a whole number of at least 0, 0 by default); of equal priorities, the one whose colour times intensity is greatest, the first added of equals. A priority that is not a whole number of at least 0 is refused (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT), and so is one on a light that is not directional. A saved world keeps it, and the sun part of the sky takes it as a field.

const sun = light.directional({ intensity: 10, position: [-50, 70, 0] })
const lamp = light.directional({ intensity: 30, position: [20, 40, 0] }) // brighter: the fog follows it
world.scene.add(sun, lamp)
sun.forwardShadingPriority = 1 // the sun now, whatever the lamp's brightness; a write reaches the world at once
world.scene.sky = { clouds: true, sun: { forwardShadingPriority: 1 } } // the sky's own sun, the same field

No bound on the light count: a 16×16 screen tile lists up to 64 lights reaching it, past that exactly those reaching it. Past 64 shadow slices a caster lights without a shadow (shadowCastersUnsliced).

Reference: world.rectLightAtlas.

light-functions.title: Light functions
light-functions.description: Give a light a material that scales its colour at each point it reaches: a window, a leaf canopy, a moving cloud.
light-functions.html:
A light can wear a light function: a material that gives, at each point the light reaches, a factor on its colour, to cast the shape of a window, a leaf canopy or a moving cloud. It is a material of the engine's one material system, made as material.lightFunction; the colour it gives is its emission: emissive times emissiveIntensity, times emissiveMap read at the coordinate of the light's projection across its tile (0 to 1), with the map's own wrap, filters, repeat, offset and rotation. White, no effect, by default. It has no world position and no depth: it is drawn once, whatever the lights that wear it, into one atlas the lighting, the volumetric fog and the translucent layers read. The map joins the materials' colour atlas, within the texture budget, and the slot is drawn again until the map is read at the detail the slot shows. A material made by another member is refused (TypeError), and a mesh refuses a light function material (INVALID_MATERIAL). A material graph wired to its emissive output replaces the parameters.

import { material, light, Texture } from 'trillion3d'

const window = material.lightFunction({ emissiveMap: new Texture(frameImage) }) // a window's panes
const lamp = light.spot({ intensity: 60, position: [0, 4, 0], distance: 20, outerConeAngle: 0.6 })
lamp.lightFunction = window // the light now shines through it
lamp.lightFunctionScale.set(4, 4, 4) // metres a tile: up, right, along the light (10.24 each by default)
lamp.lightFunctionFadeDistance = 200 // metres from the eye past which it fades (1000 by default)
lamp.lightFunctionDisabledBrightness = 0.5 // what the light is where it is faded out (0.5 by default)
window.emissive = 0xffcc66 // a warm tint, written to every light that wears it
sun.lightFunction = window // a sun projects it along its direction
rectLamp.lightFunctionConeAngle = 30 // a rectangle: through a cone of 30 degrees (0, flat, by default)

How a light projects it: a spot maps its cone to the tile (the edge of the cone is the edge of the tile at any distance); a point light maps the tile around itself by longitude and latitude; a rectangle by its face's plane, or through lightFunctionConeAngle (at most 89 degrees) like a spot; a sun by its axes, the tile repeating every lightFunctionScale. The function fades to lightFunctionDisabledBrightness over the last fifth of lightFunctionFadeDistance from the eye. The declared form is world.addLight({ id, kind, ..., lightFunction: id, lightFunctionScale: [4, 4, 4] }); a scale of three numbers above 0, a fade distance above 0, a brightness of 0 or more and, for a rect, a cone angle of 0 or more are checked, and any of these beside no lightFunction is refused (INVALID_SCENE_LIGHT).

world.lightFunction holds the settings of the atlas, each an option of createWorld too, with the reference's default: lightFunctionAtlas (true, the whole system), lightFunctionSlotResolution (128 texels a side of a slot, at least 32), lightFunctionAtlasSize (4 slots a side, from 2 to 16: 16 materials at the default; a light whose material has no slot left has none), lightFunctionMaxLights (-1, no limit: the most lights that read the atlas, the nearest to the eye, suns first, kept), lightFunctionFormat ('grey', the mean of the colour; or 'colour'), and which passes read the atlas: lightFunctionDeferred (true, the lighting of the opaque image and the translucency volume's injection), lightFunctionFog (true, the volumetric fog's local lights; its sun always reads it), lightFunctionBounce (true, the lights of the bounce: the probes' rays and the screen probes' scene traces) and lightFunctionTranslucent (false, the translucent layers).

world.lightFunction = { lightFunctionAtlasSize: 8, lightFunctionSlotResolution: 256 } // 64 sharper slots
world.lightFunction = { lightFunctionTranslucent: true, lightFunctionFormat: 'colour' } // glass, coloured
world.lightFunction = { lightFunctionFog: false } // the fog's lamps shine plain; its sun keeps its function
world.lightFunction = { lightFunctionBounce: false } // the bounce lights its surfaces with plain lamps

The bounce reads the function at the surface a probe's ray hits: a lamp whose function dims that point gives it less light, and one that dims it wholly casts no shadow ray there. A function that moves (a material that reads time) or changes makes the probes trace again, at each image it does.

Reference: world.lightFunction.

light-range.title: A lamp's range is authored, and no frame shortens it
light-range.description: A lamp's range is authored: where its influence ends, and why no frame shortens it.
light-range.html:
range is the lamp's attenuation radius in metres: influence ends there through the window (1 − (d/range)⁴)², and a point or spot shadow map is built to it. The page sets it (light.distance); unset, the world derives one from the scene's extent. Every path — the world, a source file, addLight, setLight — stores it as-is: no exposure, curve or threshold shortens it.

capability.lighting(world) reports what the active engine applies — { shadows, reason? } — not what the contract accepts; declared lights, the lighting view and node moves always apply at the next frame; reason names in one sentence what is not applied.

mesh-cast-shadow.title: Every mesh casts a shadow unless it says castShadow = false
mesh-cast-shadow.description: Every opaque mesh casts a shadow under a casting light, unless it says castShadow is false.
mesh-cast-shadow.html: Under a casting light (the light's castShadow: true, false by default), every opaque mesh casts (a mesh's castShadow defaults to true). mesh.castShadow = false, written any time, leaves every shadow map; the mesh still receives shadows. An outline drawn as a larger copy of its part wants it off, or it shades the part.

cast-shadow-maps-per-primitive.title: One primitive out of the shadow maps: castsShadowMaps = false
cast-shadow-maps-per-primitive.description: Leave one primitive of a model out of the shadow maps with castsShadowMaps.
cast-shadow-maps-per-primitive.html:
A model's mesh of several primitives (one material each) is a group of one mesh per primitive, and each of those meshes has its own castsShadowMaps, true by default. Set false, that primitive leaves the lights' shadow maps and, while another primitive of its model casts into them, nothing else: the distance fields, the global illumination, the contact shadows and the views still hold it, and it still receives shadows. A model none of whose primitives casts into the maps casts nothing at all, the distance fields' shadows included, as one mesh does: a model of one primitive set false is such a model. castShadow gates first, whole: a mesh with castShadow = false casts none whatever castsShadowMaps says. A translucent surface is never in the shadow maps, so the switch is for opaque and masked primitives.

// `model` is a loaded model; the thin trim along a cornice costs pages of shadow for a shadow
// nobody reads: out of the shadow maps, still drawn and still lit, the rest of the model casting.
const trim = model.getObjectByName('Cornice_Trim')!
trim.castsShadowMaps = false

const rail = object.mesh(geometry.box(2, 0.02, 0.02)) // a mesh of your own: alone, it casts nothing
rail.castsShadowMaps = false

A write is told to the world like castShadow: the shadow cache stales the pages the primitive was drawn in, and a row of a streamed cell takes the value of its source mesh. A clone, a model node and a saved scene keep it (a saved scene writes it only when it is false).

sun-shadow-distance.title: A sun's shadow distance and its far casters
sun-shadow-distance.description: How far a sun's shadows reach, how the view scales that distance, and the far casters beyond it.
sun-shadow-distance.html:
A directional light's shadows follow the eye. A sun has a shadow distance: shadowDistance, in metres, 400 by default, true the same, false or 0 none. The distance is the sun's own and the view scales it (shadowDistanceScale). It lays the sun's shadow levels and the edge where its distance-field cascade begins; it does not leave a caster out of the shadow maps. The reference's far-shadow test reaches the subjects it gathers on the CPU, which are no cluster geometry, and every caster the engine draws is made of clusters: the shadow maps take each of them at any distance, whether its object casts far shadows or not; no distance-field shadow takes it in their place on the view.

farShadowCulling decides whether the sun has a near edge and the distance-field cascade that follows it. The reference's far-shadow test would act on a caster that is no cluster geometry, of which the engine has none: it has no switch for the test, nor a per-object one.

The edge lies a little past the distance: the far end of the last of the sun's near shadow levels, with the overlap that level has into the next when another level follows. The levels are the sun's own settings, each with the default of a directional light:

Light optionDefaultMeaning
shadowCascades4the near levels the distance is cut into (at most the view's shadowNearLevels)
shadowCascadeExponent3how many times the span of the level before each takes
shadowCascadeTransition0.1the share of its span a level overlaps into the next
farShadowCascades0far levels between the distance and farShadowDistance, while that is more than a metre farther: counted, never drawn (the shadow maps take every cluster caster at any distance); a light that has some ends its near levels with the overlap
farShadowDistance3000 mwhere those levels end
distanceFieldShadowstruewhether the distance-field cascade follows the near levels
distanceFieldShadowDistance512 mwhere that cascade ends (true the default, false none)

The edge at the defaults is 427.0 m (400 m, near plane 0.05 m): the last level starts at 130.03 m and overlaps 27 m into the cascade that follows; the distance itself from 512 m on.

const sun = light.directional({ castShadow: true, shadowDistance: 600, shadowCascades: 3 })
sun.shadowDistance = 250 // metres, from the next frame; the light is made again, its cached pages drawn again
sun.distanceFieldShadowDistance = false // no distance-field cascade after the near levels

The view's settings sit beside them, each an option of createWorld too, resolved over the quality preset like the raster's:

View optionDefaultMeaning
shadowDistanceScale1 (0 to 2)the factor on every sun's distance, so 0.5 halves it; 0 leaves the test nothing to cull
farShadowCullingtruewhether a sun has a near edge and the distance-field cascade that follows it
shadowNearLevels10 (0 to 10)the most near levels; 0 leaves no edge: nothing is culled
shadowOverlapScale1 (0 to 2)the factor on the overlap
shadowFarFieldtruewhether the distance-field cascade follows the near levels, where the scene has distance fields
shadowMaxFarCascades10the most far levels a light may count (farShadowCascades)
shadowFarDistanceOverride0metres, where far levels end for every light when above 0; no far level is drawn, so it has no visible effect
distanceFieldDistanceScale1 (0.0001 to 10000)the factor on every light's distance-field distance

A distance-field cascade needs two things besides its row: the sun's distanceFieldShadows, and a scene whose meshes have distance fields (the mesh build's distanceField, on by default). Without fields the edge is the distance itself (400 m).

const world = createWorld('viewer', { shadowDistanceScale: 0.85, distanceFieldDistanceScale: 2 })
world.shadows = { farShadowCulling: false } // no near edge, no distance-field cascade, from the next frame
world.shadows = { farShadowCulling: null } // back to the default

One more setting of the view is the gate every light's shadow passes: shadowQuality (5, a whole number from 0 to 5). At 0 no light takes a shadow, the sun's included: no shadow map, page or trace is planned, no page pool is made (one made before is freed, its cache with it), the lit passes read no shadow and drop their shadow code, so a scene that asks for none pays nothing for them. At 1 to 5 every light takes the same shadow: the shadow maps have one method, so the levels above 0 differ in nothing today. A light that declares castsShadow keeps the declaration: the setting takes the shadow away, never the flag, and a scene turned back to a level above 0 draws its shadows again from a cache of its own. The setting does not reach the indirect light's own occlusion of a light (the bounce probes trace a ray toward each shadow-casting light, as before) nor the clouds' shadow on the sun.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { shadowQuality: 0 }) // no light takes a shadow
world.shadows = { shadowQuality: 3 } // from the next frame: every light does
world.shadows = { shadowQuality: null } // back to the default, 5
world.quality.preset = 'smooth' // the first level: no shadow at all, unless the page set one

classic-shadow-map-atlas.title: Classic shadow maps' depth atlas
classic-shadow-map-atlas.description: The depth atlas the classic shadow maps are drawn into when the virtual shadow maps are off.
classic-shadow-map-atlas.html:
With shadowVirtualEnable: false the lights' classic shadow maps are drawn into a depth atlas (a tile a map, a layer for the movable casters and one for the static casters) and joined to the page pool the readers sample. Eight options set it, with the reference defaults: shadowCsmCaching (false: a sun's cascades are drawn whole each image; true keeps the pages a sliding cascade still covers, until it has slid so far that less than shadowCsmScrollingOverlapAreaThrottle of its cached area is covered (0.75), or the last slide had to draw more than shadowMaxCsmScrollingStaticSubjects static casters again (5), and then draws its cache again whole; while the cascades are cached their casters take no slope bias), shadowCacheWholeScene (true, the static depths are kept from one image to the next), shadowCachedCastFromMovable (true; false leaves the movable casters out of the point and spot lights' shadows), shadowMaxPointCacheUpdatesPerFrame and shadowMaxSpotCacheUpdatesPerFrame (-1, no limit: past the limit a light whose resolution changed keeps its previous resolution that frame) and shadowWholeSceneCacheMb (150, the memory of every atlas of both layers, counted as 32-bit depth: the maps that do not fit are drawn into the pool without a tile; a sun's cascades never go without: their resolution shadowMaxCsmResolution is held to the atlas side less one page, so a cascade the atlas cannot hold is drawn in a coarser clipmap level). The atlas is drawn into only while the maps are classic, and costs nothing otherwise.

const world = createWorld('viewer', { shadowVirtualEnable: false }) // classic maps, drawn into the atlas
world.shadows = { shadowCsmCaching: true } // cascades reuse the pages they still cover as they slide
world.shadows = { shadowCsmScrollingOverlapAreaThrottle: 0.5, shadowMaxCsmScrollingStaticSubjects: 10 } // slide further before the cache is drawn again
world.shadows = { shadowMaxSpotCacheUpdatesPerFrame: 2 } // at most two spot lights change their resolution a frame
world.shadows = { shadowCachedCastFromMovable: false } // movable casters leave the point and spot lights' shadows
world.shadows = { shadowWholeSceneCacheMb: 300 } // a larger atlas: more room for the lights' tiles

clipmap-statistics.title: Clipmap statistics
clipmap-statistics.description: Write the statistics of a sun's shadow clipmap over the image.
clipmap-statistics.html:
shadowShowClipmapStats (-1, off) writes over the image, in the upper left, the statistics of the sun shadow clipmap of that index (0 the first): for each level the rect of pages its map has allocated (the lowest and highest page of each axis), then, where the rect is not empty, its width, its height and its area in pages, and last the total area of the levels. The rects are copied from the page management's table and read a few images late, so the figures follow the view with a short delay.

world.shadows = { shadowShowClipmapStats: 0 } // the first sun's clipmap: allocated page rects and total area
world.shadows = { shadowShowClipmapStats: -1 } // off

clusters-table.title: Clusters table
clusters-table.description: Write the statistics of the virtual shadow maps over the image: the sections and the options that name them.
clusters-table.html:
shadowShowStats ('', none) names the sections of the virtual shadow maps' statistics written over the image: 'all' or '1' every section, 'basic' the basic ones, else section names separated by commas, case ignored. The clusters section lists, at the lower left, every shadow map that drew clusters: its id, its light's name and the clusters it drew (the hardware and software raster's, summed); a map stays listed for 180 images after its last cluster. The clusters are counted by the raster while the section is shown, and read a few images late.

world.shadows = { shadowShowStats: 'clusters' } // the clusters each shadow map draws
world.shadows = { shadowShowStats: 'all' }
world.shadows = { shadowShowStats: null } // off

The shadow casters view (virtual-shadow-map-shadow-casters) paints each pixel in the colour of its placement's class, shaded by the angle of its face to the view, with the boxes of the invalidating placements over it.

shadowVisualizeLayout (0), shadowVisualizeCachedPagesOnly (false), shadowVisualizeLightName ('') and shadowVisualizeOverdrawScale (15) shape the virtual shadow map views above (virtual-shadow-map-shadow-factor and the nine others, which draw what the last ray of each pixel read). The layout is 0 over the whole image (in grey), 1 in a thumbnail of a third of the image's width and height at its upper left, 2 over its left half. shadowVisualizeCachedPagesOnly makes the cached-page view show the kept pages for every light and hide the others. shadowVisualizeLightName is the name of the one light to show, alone and in full colour: the light whose name is exactly that, else the first whose name contains it; the empty string (the default), or a name no light bears, shows every light, a quarter of each colour added. The local lights are shown with the one-pass projection (shadowOnePassProjection, on by default) and without it.

await engine.setDiagnostic('virtual-shadow-map-cached-page')
world.shadows = { shadowVisualizeLayout: 2 } // the view over the left half of the image
world.shadows = { shadowVisualizeLightName: 'Lamp', shadowVisualizeCachedPagesOnly: true } // the kept pages of the light named Lamp
world.shadows = { shadowVisualizeLayout: null, shadowVisualizeLightName: null } // back to the defaults

The overdraw view (virtual-shadow-map-overdraw) counts, in a slice of the page pool made for it, how many times the shadow raster drew each texel this image: the hardware raster for the triangles it draws and the software raster for the small ones, a draw counted wherever its pixel lands on a page that is drawn, before any depth test. Each pixel is coloured by the count of the texel it reads, 1 - 2^(-count x scale / 100) on an inferno colour map, the lights' counts added when every light is shown. shadowVisualizeOverdrawScale is that scale as a percentage (15 by default, from 0 to 100): a larger value reaches the bright end with fewer draws. The pixels that face away from their light are kept, as the counts concern the raster and not the projection. Choosing the view makes the pool again with the extra slice (and leaving it makes it without), so the cached pages are drawn again once; the software raster counts only on a device that grants eleven storage buffers a shader stage, the hardware raster on every device.

await engine.setDiagnostic('virtual-shadow-map-overdraw')
world.shadows = { shadowVisualizeOverdrawScale: 40 } // the bright end after fewer draws
world.shadows = { shadowVisualizeOverdrawScale: null } // back to 15

The quality levels (the shadows group) write the four that shape the distance and its edge, the shadow maps' rows and the shadow quality, as the rules' own rows (SHADOW_PRESET_LEVELS, packages/sdk-core/src/contracts/shadowOptions.ts):

levelshadowDistanceScaleshadowNearLevelsshadowOverlapScaleshadowFarFieldshadowQualityedge at 400 m
smooth0.610off0240.0 m
balanced0.710.25off3280.0 m
fine0.8540.8on5358.4 m
maxnothing (1)nothing (10)nothing (1)nothing (on)nothing (5)427.0 m
cinematic1101on5427.0 m

(edge at a near plane of 0.05 m.) A value the page set holds over a preset: a smooth preset draws no shadow at all, and a page that sets shadowQuality: 5 brings them back over it. A value of another kind, or out of its range, is refused by name. A change of a light's own setting (its distance, its cascades) makes the light again and its cached pages are drawn again; a change of the view's settings moves the edge the next frame's test reads, and the cached pages are kept.

The sun's distance-field shadow

A sun's shadow maps draw every cluster at any distance, and every mesh the engine draws is made of clusters, so the view traces no distance-field shadow of the sun: the cascade past the near levels (from their end to distanceFieldShadowDistance) moves the far-shadow edge, and shadows nothing by itself. The distance fields of the meshes shade the sun where the maps do not reach: the surface cache's cards, whose direct light traces a ray through the meshes listed by tile across each sun. These settings act on that list and on the cascade's edge:

View optionDefaultMeaning
distanceFieldShadowingtruewhether a sun may have a distance-field shadow cascade at all: the master switch of the feature; off, none is drawn
distanceFieldShadowQuality3 (0 to 3)the steps of a ray: 0 none, 1 twenty, 2 thirty-two, 3 sixty-four
distanceFieldShadowTileSize2 mthe side of the tiles across the light the meshes are listed in
distanceFieldShadowTwoSidedBias1the factor on the distance a two-sided mesh's surface is expanded by
distanceFieldShadowObjectsPerTile128the meshes a tile has room for on average; a tile past it loses meshes (its shadow flickers)
distanceFieldShadowCompactTilestruethe tiles' lists lie one after the other; false: each tile has a place of its own and a tile past it loses meshes
distanceFieldShadowSnapResolution2048 (at least 32)the texels across the lists' shadow space the origin's snap grid is cut from (4 texels a step, 4 texels off each side): the tile grid moves in steps with the camera

The lists are made before the surface cache's lighting, as long as the scene has a mesh with a distance field and a sun casts a shadow, for the first four shadowed lights of a frame. A merged shell's field is listed exactly where the shell is drawn: a cell shown instead of its actor, or an actor not loaded, casts nothing through it.

An object that is not to be in that scene sets affectDistanceFieldLighting (boolean, true), a property of every object, saved with the world: false leaves it out of the distance fields altogether, so that the global field the screen probes march and the distance-field shadows hold nothing of it, and its pixels carry no mark of having a distance field (the screen probes' traces then treat them as thicker, screenProbeThicknessScaleWithoutField). An object is in the scene only where it also casts a shadow (castShadow) and its mesh has a distance field.

// A decal-thin sign that must not stand in the distance fields: it neither shadows nor blocks the probes' rays.
sign.affectDistanceFieldLighting = false
const world = createWorld('viewer', {
  distanceFieldShadowQuality: 2, // 32 steps a ray
})
world.shadows = { distanceFieldShadowTileSize: 4 } // fewer, larger tiles: cheaper lists, more meshes a tile
world.shadows = { distanceFieldShadowCompactTiles: false } // each tile has a place of its own in the lists

An agent sets the same through trillion3d_set_shadows, and a light's distance and cascades through the fields of trillion3d_add_light (shadowDistance, shadowCascades, shadowCascadeExponent, shadowCascadeTransition, farShadowCascades, farShadowDistance, distanceFieldShadows, distanceFieldShadowDistance, with true for the default and false for none where a distance).

see-through-surface-shadow.title: A see-through surface casts no shadow
see-through-surface-shadow.description: A see-through surface casts no shadow: what a blended material does and does not draw into the shadow maps.
see-through-surface-shadow.html: A blended material (transparent: true) lets light pass, as glass, smoke and a light beam do, and draws nothing into the shadow maps: material.meshStandard({ transparent: true, opacity: 0.5 }) casts no shadow, whatever its opacity. An opaque or cutout surface behind it still casts its own.

see-through-surface-sun-shadow.title: A see-through surface reads the sun's shadow, with one sample
see-through-surface-sun-shadow.description: How a blended or transmissive surface reads a sun's shadow with one sample: the three project switches.
see-through-surface-sun-shadow.html:
A blended or transmissive surface is lit light by light in its own fragment: no mask holds it, so it reads each light's shadow map itself. Three project switches say how. They are shadow settings (createWorld options, world.shadows, trillion3d_set_shadows), read once when the session opens (changing them later changes nothing, as for cloudShadowOnTranslucent), and no quality level writes them:

  • shadowTranslucentQuality (0, or 1): at 0, one sample of the light's map at the surface's point, with no ray, the cheap read every layer of a blend can pay; at 1, the full trace the opaque surfaces get (rays across the light, a screen ray for contact, a dither on the share in a penumbra), at a high cost for every translucent pixel, and the sun's pages the trace reads are also marked for the nearest translucent surface the image before drew in front of each pixel.
  • shadowTranslucentLocalLights (false): whether a point, spot or rectangle light's shadow reaches the surface. Off, a shadowed local light lights it unshadowed and the translucent programs hold none of the local lights' shadow code; the sun's shadow always reaches it. On, the local lights are read as shadowTranslucentQuality says.
